check:0:0.q: Why not “The token price, because it is on the monthly b…”?
check:0:0.a:
It's a fair instinct. The token price is real money, and it shows up on the bill every month. It's also easy to see, which makes it feel important. You should still keep an eye on it.

But this lesson asks a different question. It isn't "which cost is most visible?" It's "which guess, if we got it wrong, would change the answer most?" That's what the **swing** tells you: how far the monthly value moves when one guess goes from its bad value to its good one.

Doubling the token price moves the value by about $390. Even if your price guess is way off, the plan barely changes. Measuring it carefully in the POC (the proof of concept, a small trial run) would teach you very little.

The success rate swings the value by $18,900. That's about 48 times bigger. If the AI is right only 50 in 100 times, the plan could fall apart. That's the guess to pin down.

"How often the AI is right, on labelled past tickets" is better because it targets the guess with the biggest swing, and it measures that guess against real, hand-checked answers.

check:0:1.q: Why not “The fixed monthly costs, because they come ever…”?
check:0:1.a:
That answer has one thing right. Fixed costs are real, and they come off the value every month. A plan has to count them.

But "comes every month" isn't what makes a guess worth measuring. Every part of this plan is monthly. Tasks, savings and the token bill all repeat each month too. So repeating doesn't set fixed costs apart.

What matters is the **swing**: how far the answer moves when you change one guess from its bad value to its good value. Fixed costs are usually well known already, because they come from contracts and quotes. A guess you already know well has a small swing, so a trial learns little by measuring it.

The question gives you the swings to compare. Token price moves the value by about $390. How often the AI is right moves it by $18,900. That second one is the guess that can sink the plan. It's also the one nobody knows yet.

"How often the AI is right, on labelled past tickets" is better because it measures the guess with the biggest swing, using real tickets where the right answer is already known.

judge.notes: The claim that fixed costs are usually well known from contracts and quotes is not in the lesson, which treats every input as an assumption. It doesn't contradict the lesson, but it is the main reason given for ruling out fixed costs.

check:1:0.q: Why not “Nothing: two at a time is faster”?
check:1:0.a:
It's true that moving two guesses together means fewer runs, so it is faster. But speed isn't the goal. The goal is to find **which** guess matters most, and moving two at once hides that.

Here's why. Say the teammate drops the task count from 6000 to 3000 and success from 0.8 to 0.5 at the same time. The monthly value falls from $23,600 to $500. That's a big drop. But which guess caused it? You can't split the drop between them.

Try them one at a time instead:

- Success at 0.5 alone gives $11,000. That's a drop of $12,600.
- Tasks at 3000 alone gives $6,800. That's a drop of $16,800.

Notice that these two drops don't add up to the combined drop. The guesses multiply together in the formula, so their effects tangle. That's another reason a joint move can't be pulled apart afterwards.

So "Nothing" misses the whole point. A faster answer that can't tell you what to measure isn't useful.

"You can't tell which guess moved it" is better because a sensitivity analysis only works when each swing belongs to one guess, so you can compare the swings and measure the biggest one hardest.

check:1:1.q: Why not “They should move every guess at once”?
check:1:1.a:
"They should move every guess at once" gets one thing right. Moving all the guesses together to their bad values, then to their good values, is a real and useful check. It shows the full range the plan could land in, from the **worst case** to the **best case**.

But it doesn't fix the teammate's problem. It makes it worse. The teammate moved two guesses together, so when the monthly value dropped, nobody could say which guess caused the drop. Move every guess and the answer still moves, but the blame is now spread across all of them.

A **sensitivity analysis** has one job: find the guess with the biggest **swing**, meaning how far the answer moves when that one guess goes from bad to good. To see each guess's own swing, you change only that guess and hold the others at their expected values. Then you can compare swings and know where to spend your trial, such as hand-labelling 50 tickets to measure `success`.

"You can't tell which guess moved it" is better because it names the real flaw: changing guesses together hides each one's swing.

judge.notes: Minor: the claim that moving all guesses to worst or best together is a 'real and useful check' goes slightly beyond the lesson, though it doesn't contradict it. The answer is about 186 words, so it fits the limit.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Ask staff how good they think it will be”?
check:2:1.a:
Asking staff is cheap and quick, and that part is right. Staff know the tickets well. They might warn you about tricky cases, like policy questions with exceptions, and that is useful to hear.

But their answer is still a guess. You would be swapping one guess for another. The whole point of the sensitivity analysis was to find the guess with the biggest swing, here `success`, and replace it with something real. An opinion can't do that.

People are also poor at judging AI accuracy in their heads. Some expect it to be nearly perfect. Others expect it to fail at everything. Either way, the number you put in the plan could be badly off. And with this guess, a wrong number moves the value anywhere from $11,000 to $29,900.

Opinions also can't be checked or repeated. If someone asks "how do you know it's 80 in 100?", "staff said so" is weak.

Trying the prompt on 50 past tickets labelled by hand (each one marked by a person with the correct answer) is better. It is still cheap, and it gives you a measured share of right answers that you can put in place of the `success` guess.

judge.notes: Passes, but it is right at the ~200-word limit, and the claim that people judge AI accuracy poorly goes beyond the lesson, though it doesn't contradict it.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Read the model maker's benchmark scores”?
check:2:2.a:
Reading the model maker's benchmark scores is cheap, and that part is right. A **benchmark** is a standard test the maker runs on its model, such as maths puzzles or general knowledge questions. The scores are free to read and give a rough idea of how capable the model is in general.

But they don't measure your guess. The `success` guess is "how often the AI is right on *our* HR tickets, with *our* prompt." A benchmark uses someone else's questions, someone else's prompt, and none of your company's policies. A model can score well there and still get your tickets wrong. The maker also picks which tests to publish, so the numbers may lean flattering.

That matters most here. This guess has the biggest swing in the plan, from $11,000 to $29,900. So it deserves a real measurement, not a borrowed one.

Trying the prompt on 50 past tickets labelled by hand is better because it is still cheap, and it measures the exact thing the plan depends on: your tickets, your prompt, and your idea of a correct answer.

judge.notes: The claim that makers choose which tests to publish goes beyond the lesson, but it does not contradict it.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Move one guess, keep the biggest” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "A business case rests on guesses, called assumptions. Examples are how many tasks there are, how often the AI is right, and how much each task saves. A trial can't measure everything. So teams often measure the easy things and miss the one guess that sinks the plan."

*The idea:* "I run a sensitivity analysis. I move one guess from its worst case to its best case. I keep the others at their expected value. The swing is how far the result moves. In an HR example, the AI's success rate swung the monthly value by about $18,900. Doubling the token price cost only about $390. So I'd measure success first, by testing the prompt on 50 hand-labelled past tickets with MLflow."

*The trade-off:* "Moving one guess at a time misses guesses that make each other worse. Low success and high costs together can hurt more than either alone."

**Likely follow-up:** "Where do your low and high values come from?"

*Hint:* Agree them with the business owner before you start, so nobody picks them to suit the answer. Then swap the biggest-swing guess for a measured number.

judge.notes: No real problems. The $18,900 swing (50% to 95% success) is set beside the $390 cost of doubling the token price, so the two ranges differ. The one-at-a-time trade-off is the tutor's own addition, though it does not contradict the lesson.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The trial measured the easy things.** You have exact token costs and task counts. But `success`, how often the AI is right, is still a number someone picked in a meeting.
- **The value collapses after launch.** The plan promised about $23,600 a month. Real use delivers closer to $11,000. Often the cause is a hit rate that was never tested on real tickets.
- **The swings look odd.** Every guess shows a similar swing. That can mean two guesses were moved at once, or the low and high values were set too close together. A swing below zero means the gap wasn't made positive.
- **No one agreed the ranges.** The worst, base and best cases came from one person, not from you and the business owner together.

**Quickest check**

Make a small table. Give each guess one row with its low, base and high value and its swing. Sort the rows by swing, biggest first. Look at the top row. Has that guess been measured, for example on 50 hand-labelled past tickets? Or is it still a guess? If it's still a guess, the analysis was skipped where it mattered most.

judge.notes: No serious problems. Minor: 'Every guess shows a similar swing' is not in the lesson and is not always a sign of error, and 'hit rate' is not defined.

learn:stops.a:
One-guess-at-a-time works well for a first look. Here are three places it needs extra care.

**Guesses that move together.** Sometimes guesses are linked. More tasks might mean harder tickets, so `success` drops as `tasks` rises. Changing one at a time hides this. Also test a few combined scenarios, such as "everything bad at once," to see the real downside.

**Cliffs in the middle.** The method only checks the low and high ends. But value may not change smoothly. If staff stop trusting the AI below 70 in 100 right, value could collapse at that point. Check a few middle values too, and ask the business owner where the cliffs are.

**Guesses that drift over time.** A share measured on 50 past tickets is a snapshot. New ticket types, policy changes or a model update can change it. A share from only 50 tickets is also rough. So re-run the evaluation on fresh hand-labelled tickets regularly. Then update the plan with the new number.

judge.notes: No real problems; each point runs slightly over the 2-3 sentence guide (the drift point has about five), but the content is accurate, plain and about 165 words.

learn:term.q: How is “worst case” different from “base case”?
learn:term.a:
**Base case** is your expected value for a guess: the number you think is most likely. **Worst case** is a bad but still believable value for that same guess. You and the business owner agree on both, along with a **best case** (a good but believable value).

Think of a commute. Most days it takes 30 minutes. That's your base case. On a bad-traffic day it takes 50. That's your worst case. You plan around 30, but you want to know how late a bad day could make you.

They work together in the sensitivity analysis. Every guess starts at its base case. Then you move just one guess to its worst case, then to its best case, and see how far the answer moves. That gap is the **swing**.

In the HR example, `tasks` stays at 6000, `saving` at 7 and `fixed` at 10000. The base case for `success` is 0.8, which gives about $23,600 a month. Its worst case is 0.5, which drops the value to $11,000. Its best case is 0.95, which gives $29,900. So the swing for `success` is $18,900.

check:0:0.q: Why not “The cheaper model still sends the same number o…”?
check:0:0.a:
That option is partly true. A cheaper model may well use about the same number of **tokens** (the small chunks of text a model reads and writes). But it does not explain the result.

The token bill is tokens times price. If the price halves and the tokens stay the same, the model's bill still halves. In the HR ticket example, it drops from 6.5 cents to about 3.25 cents. So "same number of tokens" can't be why the cost hardly moves. The bill did move.

What the option misses is the size of the other costs. A finished ticket costs about $1.865:

- model: $0.065
- **human review** (a person checking some answers): $0.60
- **rework** (redoing failed answers): $1.20

Saving about 3 cents out of $1.865 is under 2 percent. That is why the total barely changes.

"Checking and redoing answers cost far more than tokens" is the better answer. It names the real reason: the model is under 4 percent of the cost per finished task, so even halving it can't shift the total much.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Token prices only count for answers, not for pr…”?
check:0:1.a:
That option has a small grain of truth. Output tokens (the words the model writes back) often cost more each than input tokens. Tokens are the small chunks of text a model reads and writes. But the option is still wrong. You pay for prompt tokens too, the text you send in. The lesson's MLflow code counts both: `input_tokens * IN` plus `output_tokens * OUT`.

It also misses the point of the question. Even if only answers were billed, that would not explain why halving the price barely moves the total.

Look at the HR ticket numbers:

- Model: $0.065
- Checking: $0.60
- Redo: $1.20
- Total: $1.865

Halve the model cost and it drops to about $0.0325. The total becomes about $1.83. You save roughly 3 cents, under 2 percent. The checking and redo costs don't change at all, because people's time costs the same whichever model you use.

"Checking and redoing answers cost far more than tokens" is the better answer because the model is under 4 percent of a finished ticket. So even a big cut to token prices hardly changes the total.

judge.notes: No real problems; minor nits are that the closing explanation runs to two sentences rather than the requested one, and the inline `input_tokens * IN` code is slightly technical.

check:1:0.a:
The model's price list is a real source in this lesson, just not for this number.

It tells you one thing: what the model charges for tokens. Tokens are the small chunks of text the model reads and writes. That price goes into the model's share of the cost, the 6.5 cents in the HR ticket example.

But checking an answer is human work. How long it takes depends on your team, your tickets and how your HR process runs. The model's maker has no idea how fast your staff read and approve an answer. So the price list simply doesn't contain that number.

There's a second reason it matters. In the HR ticket bot, the model is under 4 percent of the cost per finished task. Checking and redoing failed answers are most of the bill. Getting the check time right moves the total far more than the token price does.

The business owner is better because they run the work, so they know how long a check takes, how many answers get checked and what an hour of staff time costs.

check:1:2.a:
"The POC's traces" sounds reasonable. The POC (proof of concept, a small trial build) is where you measure things. But traces are the wrong tool for this number.

A trace is the record MLflow saves each time the bot runs. In the lesson's code, the useful part is `token_usage`: how many tokens went in and came out. Multiply those by the price list's token prices and you get the model's cost per task. So traces are the right source for that part.

What traces don't hold is a person's checking time. The checking happens after the bot answers, by a human, outside the model run. The lesson's code says this directly: "Checking and redo costs come from the POC's review notes, not traces." So traces miss this number completely.

Then the lesson names who supplies the check details. The business owner gives the hourly rate, how many answers get checked, and how long a check takes.

"The business owner" is better because the lesson lists them as the source for how long a person takes to check one answer.

check:2:1.q: Why not “It stays the same: tokens didn't change”?
check:2:1.a:
That option gets one thing right. The tokens did not change, so the model's bill per task stays the same. A prompt fix that keeps the same tokens costs nothing extra to run.

What it misses is that tokens are only one part of the **cost per finished task**. That cost is the model's bill, plus **human review** (a person checking some answers), plus **rework** (redoing the answers that fail). In the lesson's HR ticket bot, the model is under 4 percent of the total. Most of the money sits in the people costs.

Halving failures shrinks the rework part directly. Say each redo costs $8, like the lesson's example:

- Before: 1 in 5 fails, so rework is 0.2 × $8 = $1.60 a task.
- After: 1 in 10 fails, so rework is 0.1 × $8 = $0.80 a task.

That saves 80 cents on every task. The token bill stays the same, so the total still drops.

"It goes down: less rework to pay for" is better because the cost per finished task includes paying people to redo failures, and fewer failures means less of that cost.

check:2:2.q: Why not “It goes up: fixes always cost more”?
check:2:2.a:
**Why not "It goes up: fixes always cost more"?**

This answer has one fair point. Making a fix takes some work. Someone has to rewrite and test the prompt, and some fixes do make prompts longer and pricier.

But the question rules that out. It says the tokens stay the same, so the model's bill per task does not change. The work of writing the fix happens once. It is not paid again on every ticket, so it is not part of the cost per finished task.

What the answer misses is **rework**, the cost of redoing failed answers. That cost depends on how often answers fail. Say a redo costs $8, like the HR ticket by hand:

- 1 in 5 fail: 0.2 × $8 = $1.60 a task
- Half as many, 1 in 10: 0.1 × $8 = $0.80 a task

That saves 80 cents on every task. The model's bill is the same, so nothing grows to cancel it out.

**Why "It goes down: less rework to pay for" is better:** halving the failures halves the rework cost, and nothing else in the total gets bigger, so each finished task costs less.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Add checking and redoing to the cost” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
When people price an AI task, they often look only at the token bill. That is the money the model provider charges for the text going in and out. It is usually the smallest part.

The real cost of a finished task adds two more things. First, a person checks some answers. That is **human review**. Second, someone fixes the answers that fail. That is **rework**.

If you skip these, your saving looks far bigger than it is. Then the project gets approved, the real bills arrive, and the value seems to vanish. That is one reason many AI trials get dropped.

A small example: a task costs $5 by hand today, and the model costs 10 cents. That looks like a $4.90 saving. Now add the other two costs:

- **Checking:** 40 in 100 answers get checked, 3 minutes each, at $60 an hour. That adds $1.20.
- **Redoing:** 20 in 100 answers fail and cost $5 each to redo. That adds $1.00.

The real cost is $2.30, so the true saving is $2.70. It is not $4.90. Pricing it fully up front avoids that surprise.

judge.notes: The arithmetic checks out ($1.20 checking + $1.00 redo + $0.10 model = $2.30, so a $2.70 saving). Calling it the 'true saving' slightly glosses over the separate cost of uncaught mistakes, but this is minor and nothing in it contradicts the lesson.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Add up the three costs” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* Teams often price an AI task by the model's token bill alone. That number looks tiny, so the project looks cheap. Then the real costs show up, and the project gets dropped after the trial.

*The idea:* I price a finished task instead. That's three costs added together. First, the model's tokens. Second, a person checking some answers, called human review. Third, redoing the answers that fail, called rework. In an HR ticket example, the model was under 4 percent of about $1.87 a ticket. Each number has a clear source: the price list, the trial build, or the business owner.

*An edge case:* Some wrong answers slip through unnoticed and cost money later. I keep that cost separate and take it off the saving, so it isn't counted twice.

**A likely follow-up**

"How would you bring this cost down?"

*Hint:* Don't start with a cheaper model, because it's the smallest slice. First, lower the failure rate, since each failure costs a full redo. Then, once the bot has earned trust, check fewer answers.

judge.notes: Minor only: "tokens" is not explained, and "so it isn't counted twice" is the tutor's own reason, not one the lesson states. Neither contradicts the lesson.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The saving looks too good.** The plan says a ticket costs a few cents, so nearly all of today's $8 looks saved. Later the real spend is far higher, because people's time was never counted.
- **The model is most of the cost.** In a task with human review, the model's bill is usually a small slice. In the HR ticket bot it is under 4 percent. If your token cost is close to your total, review or rework is probably missing.
- **The trial measured only tokens.** Your POC (the small trial build) reports token counts but no failure rate. Nobody wrote down how many answers were checked or how long a check took.
- **Numbers have no source.** The hourly rate or check time was guessed instead of coming from the business owner.
- **Slipped-through mistakes are counted twice.** They appear inside the cost per task and are also taken off the saving.

**Quickest check**

Rebuild one finished task by hand, the way the lesson's $1.865 example does. Add the token cost, the checking cost and the redo cost. Then see whether the model share looks plausibly small. Also confirm that every number names where it came from.

judge.notes: No real problems; the claim that the model is 'usually a small slice' goes slightly beyond the lesson (which only says under 4 percent for the HR bot), and the length is close to the 200-word limit.

learn:stops.a:
**1. When the work drifts over time.** The POC measured tokens and failure rates on today's tickets. New policies, new question types or a model update can change both. Re-check them from live traces and review notes every so often, and redo the sum when they move.

**2. When the trial was tiny.** If the POC saw only a few dozen tickets, its failure rate is a rough guess, and a small swing changes the redo cost a lot. Price a low and a high case, and ask the business owner again later, since the share they want checked may drop as trust grows.

**3. When one task makes many model calls.** An agent (a program that lets the model choose steps and use tools) may loop or retry, so some tasks cost far more tokens than others. An average can hide this. Look at the most expensive tasks too, and set a limit on steps per task.

learn:term.q: How is “fully loaded cost” different from “human review”?
learn:term.a:
They sit at different levels. One is the whole bill. The other is one line on that bill.

**Fully loaded cost** is the total cost of one finished task. It adds up three parts: the model's token bill, plus human review, plus rework (redoing the answers that fail).

**Human review** is just one of those parts. It is the cost of a person checking some of the answers. You get it from how many answers are checked, how long each check takes, and that person's hourly rate.

So human review feeds into the fully loaded cost. It is never the whole of it.

Think of a meal at a restaurant. The fully loaded cost is everything it took to put the plate on the table. Human review is like the chef tasting some dishes before they go out. It is a real cost, but only one piece.

In the HR ticket bot:

- Model: $0.065
- Human review: 30 in 100 checked, 2 minutes each, at $60 an hour = $0.60
- Rework: $1.20
- Fully loaded cost: $1.865 a ticket

Here human review costs about nine times the model's bill.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Global, because it is the cheapest”?
check:0:1.a:
"Global, because it is the cheapest" gets one thing right. Global really is the cheapest type. For `gpt-4.1` it costs $2.00 per million input tokens, against $2.20 for Data Zone or Regional. A token is a small chunk of text the model reads or writes.

What it misses is the rule. Your HR data must stay in the EU. With Global, Azure may process your requests in any Azure region, including ones outside the EU. Your stored data stays in your chosen geography whichever type you pick. But the processing could still happen elsewhere, and that breaks the rule.

So the answer skips the first step. The lesson's order is: data rules first, then model and region, then price. Price only chooses among the options that already pass the rules. Here Global is out before price even comes up. A cheaper option you are not allowed to use is not an option at all.

Data Zone EU, or Regional in the EU, is better because it keeps processing inside the EU. That follows the rule, and it costs only about 10% more.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Any type: stored data stays put”?
check:0:2.a:
That option gets one thing right. **Stored data** (the files and records Azure keeps for you) does stay in your chosen geography, whichever deployment type you pick. That part of the lesson is true.

What it misses is **processing**. Processing is the moment the model actually reads your request and works on it. Each time your app sends HR data to the model, that data travels to wherever the model runs.

With a Global deployment, that can be any Azure region in the world. So an EU employee's record might be handled in the US or Asia, even though it's stored in the EU. "Must stay in the EU" covers that moment too, so Global breaks the rule.

That's why the lesson says the data rules come first. They remove Global before price is even considered. Global being cheapest doesn't help if you aren't allowed to use it.

"Data Zone EU, or Regional in the EU" is better because both keep processing, not just storage, inside the EU, which is what the rule actually asks for.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Use Global: it is only a test”?
check:1:1.a:
"Use Global: it is only a test" gets one thing right. Trying a new model early is useful. Global is also where new models usually appear first, with the most quota (your allowed tokens per minute), and it is the cheapest type.

What it misses is that the data rule doesn't care whether you call it a test. With Global, your requests may be processed in any Azure region, including ones outside the EU. Your stored data stays in your chosen geography, but the processing does not. If your test sends real data, that data can leave the EU, and the rule is broken. Tests often use real data, because that is how you see if the model works for you.

It also flips the lesson's order. Step one is your data rules. They decide which deployment types you may use at all. Global is out before price or convenience even come up.

"Wait for it in the EU Data Zone" is better because it follows the rule first and still gets you the new model, just a little later.

judge.notes: No real problem. Minor: 'Tests often use real data' and 'just a little later' go beyond what the lesson says, but neither contradicts it.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Use Global, then delete the data”?
check:1:2.a:
**Why "Use Global, then delete the data" falls short**

It gets one thing right. It notices that the data matters, and it tries to limit the damage.

But it misses what the rule is about. A **Global** deployment may *process* your request in any Azure region. "Processing" means the model reads your prompt and works on it. So the moment you send EU data, it might be handled in the US or Asia. That is the very thing your EU-only rule forbids.

Deleting afterwards can't undo that. The data has already left the EU while it was being worked on. The rule is broken at send time, not at storage time.

There's a second gap too. The lesson says stored data stays in your chosen geography whatever type you pick. So deletion doesn't even target the risky part, which is the processing.

Remember the order: data rules first, then model and region, then price. Global fails step one, so it's out, however new or cheap it is.

**Why waiting is better:** an EU Data Zone deployment keeps processing inside the EU, so you follow the rule from the very first request instead of trying to fix it afterwards.

check:2:1.a:
"$10 a month" gets one thing right. Data Zone does cost more than Global, so the answer points the right way. But the number is ten times too small.

Here is the sum, step by step:

- The price gap is $2.20 minus $2.00. That is **$0.20** per million input tokens.
- Your app sends 500 million input tokens. That is 500 "millions."
- 500 × $0.20 = **$100**.

You can check it another way:

- Global: 500 × $2.00 = $1,000 a month.
- Data Zone: 500 × $2.20 = $1,100 a month.
- The difference is $100.

An answer of $10 usually comes from a decimal slip. Using $0.02 as the gap instead of $0.20 gives exactly $10. Another slip is reading "about 10% more" as "$10 more." The 10% is a percentage of the bill, not a fixed dollar amount. Ten percent of $1,000 is $100.

"$100 a month" is better because it multiplies the real $0.20 gap by all 500 million tokens.

check:2:2.a:
"$1,000 a month" is a real number from this question. It's just the answer to a different question.

Prices are "per million tokens." A token is a small chunk of text, often part of a word. Your app sends 500 million input tokens a month, which is 500 lots of a million.

- On Global Standard, each million costs $2.00. So 500 × $2.00 = $1,000.
- On Data Zone, each million costs $2.20. So 500 × $2.20 = $1,100.

So $1,000 is the full monthly bill on Global. The question asks what Data Zone *adds*: the extra you pay on top of Global. That number misses the last step, which is taking the difference between the two bills.

$1,100 − $1,000 = $100.

You can also get there directly. Data Zone costs $0.20 more per million, and 0.20 × 500 = $100. That matches the lesson's "about 10% more."

"$100 a month" is better because it is the gap between the two bills, which is exactly the extra cost the question asks about.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Filter by the rules, then take the cheapest” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
Here's a 30-second answer you could say out loud.

**The problem.** In Azure AI Foundry, each model deployment has a type. The type decides where requests may be processed. Global is cheapest. Data Zone and Regional cost about 10% more but keep processing inside one area. Company privacy rules may forbid some types.

**The idea.** Rules first, price last. I drop every option whose data location isn't on the allowed list. Among what's left, I take the cheapest. It's like booking a flight: first only flights that land where you need to be, then the cheapest of those. If I looked at price first, I'd grab Global and might break the rules.

**Edge case.** Sometimes nothing passes the rules. Then I report clearly that no option is allowed, instead of quietly falling back to Global.

**A follow-up an interviewer might ask:** "The cheapest allowed option has no quota in your region. What now?"

Hint: quota is the tokens per minute you may use. It's set per region, per model and per type, and it doesn't carry over between regions. A strong answer treats model availability and enough quota as part of the filter, checked before price. Bonus point: new models often reach Global first.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

The bill looks too good. Restricted data is running at $2.00 a million input tokens for gpt-4.1. That is the Global price. It may mean someone picked on price first and skipped the data rules. Global can process requests in any Azure region, so EU-only HR data would break the rules.

The privacy team flags it later. A review finds a deployment type that isn't on their allowed list. The app worked fine, so nobody noticed.

The plan fails at setup. The model you wanted isn't offered as Data Zone or Regional in your region yet. New models often come to Global first.

The app runs out of room sooner than planned. **Quota** means the tokens per minute you may use. Maybe two apps share one quota, so each gets half. Or someone assumed quota from another region would carry over. It doesn't.

**Quickest check**

List every deployment with its type and region. Compare each type to the allowed list from your data rules. Then check quota for that region, model and type. Only after both pass, confirm you chose the cheapest type left.

learn:stops.a:
The rule "filter by data rules, then take the cheapest" is a good start. Here are three places where it needs extra care.

**The cheapest allowed option has no room.** Data Zone EU might pass your rules but have too little quota (tokens per minute) for your traffic, or not offer the model yet. Check that the model exists there and that quota is enough before you compare prices. If one deployment is too small, ask for more quota or spread the load over a second allowed region.

**Things change over time.** New models usually land in Global first, and Data Zone or Regional versions come later. Prices and your privacy team's rules can also change. Don't decide once and forget it. Re-check the options when you switch models or when the rules are updated.

**Cheap but slow.** Batch costs half as much, but your results come back later, not right away. That is fine for overnight jobs. It is wrong for a chatbot a person is waiting on. Add "how fast must it answer?" as a filter before you look at price.

learn:term.a:
A **deployment type** is a setting you pick for each model in Azure AI Foundry. It decides where in the world your requests may be processed. "Processed" means the moment the model reads your prompt and writes its reply. It also changes the price.

Think of sending a parcel. You can let the courier route it through any depot in the world. That's cheapest. Or you pay a bit more to keep it inside one continent, or inside one country. The parcel arrives either way. You are choosing the route, and the route sets the price.

The lesson names three types:

- `Global`: any Azure region. A region is one group of data centres, like East US.
- `Data Zone`: only inside the US, the EU or Asia Pacific.
- `Regional`: only inside one geography you choose.

Your stored data stays in your chosen geography whichever type you pick. The type only covers processing.

In the HR example, the data must stay in the EU. `Global` could process requests anywhere, so it's ruled out, even though it's cheapest at $2.00. Of the types left, `Data Zone EU` is the cheapest at $2.20.

judge.notes: No real problems. The definition comes before the everyday comparison, though the brief asked for the comparison first, and "one country" only loosely matches "one geography".

check:0:1.q: Why not “Only new documents use the new model”?
check:0:1.a:
It sounds sensible. Why pay to redo work you've already done? And part of it is true: after the switch, new documents do go through the new model.

What it misses is that vectors (the lists of numbers an embedding makes) from two different models can't be compared. Each model has its own way of turning meaning into numbers. Their numbers don't line up.

Here is why that matters. Every question also becomes a vector before the search. After the switch, the question's vector comes from the new model. The old documents still have vectors from the old model. The search would be comparing numbers that don't share a meaning, so it can't tell which old documents match.

So the old documents have to be embedded again with the new model. That is one more full pass over every document, paid once. It is a one-off cost, like the first time you built the index. How big it is depends on the new model's price per token.

"Every document is embedded again, once" is better because it names the real extra cost: one full re-embedding, paid once, so every vector comes from the same model.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Nothing: the old vectors still work”?
check:0:2.a:
It is a tempting answer, and it gets one thing right. The old vectors don't break or vanish. They still work fine, as long as you keep using the old model.

The catch is that a **vector** (the list of numbers an embedding model makes from text) only makes sense next to other vectors from the same model. Each model has its own way of turning meaning into numbers. Once you switch, every new question becomes a vector from the new model. Comparing it with document vectors from the old model is like comparing prices in two different currencies without converting. The search would return poor matches.

So you can't keep the old document vectors. Every document has to go through the new model again. That is one more full pass, priced like the first build: the documents times their tokens times the new model's price per token. Your monthly bill can change too, because new documents and questions are now billed at the new model's price.

"Every document is embedded again, once" is better because it names the real cost: one full re-embedding, since vectors from two models can't be compared.

check:1:1.a:
"$1.50" is ten times too big. The method behind it is usually right. The slip is in the size of the numbers.

What it gets right: you multiply the questions by their tokens, then multiply by the price. That is the correct order of steps.

Where it goes wrong: one zero sneaks in somewhere. Here is the sum done slowly.

1. Count the tokens: 300,000 questions times 25 tokens = 7,500,000 tokens. That is 7.5 million.
2. Price per million is $0.02, so 7.5 times $0.02 = $0.15.

To get $1.50, you would need 75 million tokens, not 7.5 million. Or you might divide by 100,000 instead of by a million. Both are easy slips when a number has this many zeros.

A quick habit helps. First write the token count in millions, here 7.5. Then multiply by the price per million. A small number of millions keeps the zeros from wandering.

"$0.15" is better because it is exactly 7.5 million tokens times $0.02 per million, with no extra zero added.

check:1:2.a:
"$150" gets the first step right. It counts the tokens correctly: 300,000 questions times 25 tokens is 7,500,000 tokens a month. It also multiplies by the price, which is the right move.

The slip is in the last step. The price is $0.02 per *million* tokens. "$150" is what you get if you divide by a thousand instead of a million, as if the price were $0.02 per thousand tokens. That makes the answer a thousand times too big.

Here is the sum done the lesson's way:

- 7,500,000 tokens is 7.5 million tokens.
- 7.5 million times $0.02 is $0.15.

A quick sense check helps here. The lesson says embeddings are rarely the big cost line. $150 a month just to turn questions into vectors would be surprisingly large. That is a hint to recheck the units.

"$0.15" is better because it divides the token count by a million before multiplying by the price, which matches how the price is quoted.

check:2:1.q: Why not “Embedding the documents the first time”?
check:2:1.a:
"Embedding the documents the first time" is a real cost. You do pay it. Every chunk of every document becomes a **vector**, a list of numbers that captures meaning, when you first build the **index**, the store the search looks through. So this option is not wrong about the cost existing.

It is just hard to forget. Building the index is the first thing anyone plans, so this cost is always on the list. In the HR example it is 3,000,000 tokens, or $0.06, once.

The one that slips through is re-embedding. Vectors from two different models can't be compared. So when someone swaps in a newer embedding model, every document has to be embedded again. That is one more full pass, about the same size as the first one. It feels like a small upgrade, so nobody thinks to budget for it. But the bill arrives either way.

"Embedding everything again after a model change" is the better answer because it is a full pass that is easy to leave out of the plan. That is why the lesson says to plan for it before anyone swaps the model.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Embedding new documents each month”?
check:2:2.a:
"Embedding new documents each month" is a real cost, so it is not a wrong idea. It just isn't the one people forget.

**What it gets right:** every new document must become a vector before the search can find it. A vector is the list of numbers that stands for the text's meaning. So yes, you pay for this every month.

**What it misses:** this cost is easy to see coming. New documents arrive on a steady schedule, so it lands in the monthly budget almost by itself. It is also tiny. In the HR example, 100 new documents is 150,000 tokens. At $0.02 a million, that is about $0.003, well under one cent a month.

The forgotten cost only shows up when someone swaps the embedding model. Vectors from two different models can't be compared. So every old document has to be embedded again, in one full pass. That is the same size as the first build. Nobody plans for it, because nothing has changed in the documents themselves.

"Embedding everything again after a model change" is better because it is a full, surprise cost that hides until the swap, so it is the easiest to leave out of the plan.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Tokens times the price, once and every month” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "A RAG app turns text into vectors, which are lists of numbers, so a search can match meaning. That step is billed per token, a small piece of a word. So I need to know what it costs."

*The idea:* "I count the tokens and multiply by the price per token. I pay once to embed every document. Then I pay every month for new documents and every question. For example, 2,000 documents of 1,500 tokens at $0.02 a million comes to $0.06, once."

*The trade-off:* "A better embedding model can find better matches. But switching means embedding every document again, because vectors from two models can't be compared. So I budget that full pass before anyone swaps the model."

**A likely follow-up**

"Is embedding the biggest cost in a RAG app?"

Hint: say no, usually not. The monthly embedding bill is often just cents. The search service that stores and searches the vectors tends to cost far more. A strong answer shows you know where the real money goes.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
A few warning signs tell you the embedding cost was skipped or worked out wrong.

**Your estimate looks wildly off.** If the one-off cost for 2,000 documents comes out at $60,000 instead of cents, you probably forgot to turn the price per million into a price per token. A sum a million times too big, or too small, is the classic slip.

**The bill keeps growing after launch.** If you only priced the first build, the monthly line surprises you. Every new document and every question costs tokens too.

**A sudden spike in one month.** Someone swapped the embedding model, and every document was embedded again. That full pass was never in the plan.

**Search results turn to nonsense.** The app compares old vectors with new ones from a different model. These can't be compared, so matches look random.

**Quickest check:** do the sum by hand once. Count the tokens, multiply by the price, divide by a million. Then compare that with the token count and charge on your provider's usage page for one day. If the two numbers are close, your plan holds.

learn:stops.a:
The simple sum (tokens times price) holds up well. A few situations need extra care.

**Documents change, not just grow.** The monthly sum counts only new documents. If old documents get edited, each edited one must be embedded again, or the search returns outdated text. Count edited documents in your monthly tokens too.

**Your token count is a guess.** The sum assumes every document is about 1,500 tokens. Real documents vary a lot. If you split them into overlapping chunks (pieces that share some text at their edges), the shared text gets embedded twice. Measure a sample of your real chunks before trusting the estimate.

**The system gets much bigger.** At 2,000 documents, a full re-embedding costs pennies. At millions of documents, the one-off pass and any model swap become real money. Prices also differ by region and change over time, so recheck the pricing page. Put the full re-embedding in the budget before anyone changes the model.

judge.notes: It says "the monthly sum counts only new documents", but the lesson's monthly sum counts new documents and every question (900,000 tokens includes the 30,000 questions).

learn:term.a:
They are two sides of one step. **Embedding** is the action: a model reads text and turns it into numbers. **Vector** is what comes out: the list of numbers itself, like `[0.12, -0.48, 0.91, ...]`.

Think of a map app. You type an address, and the app works out its GPS coordinates. Working out the coordinates is the embedding. The coordinates are the vector. Two places close together have similar coordinates. In the same way, two texts with similar meaning get similar vectors, so a search can find them.

One catch: people often say "an embedding" when they mean the vector it produced. So the words get used loosely.

In the lesson's HR assistant, every chunk of the 2,000 documents gets embedded once, and that is where you pay per token. Each embedding gives back one vector. Every question also gets embedded into a vector before the search compares it with the stored ones.

The cost lives in the embedding step. The vectors are what you keep and search. Storing them is the next lesson's cost.

check:0:1.q: Why not “The name of the person who typed it”?
check:0:1.a:
Knowing who typed the line isn't useless. It gives you someone to ask, and some teams do track that. But it doesn't help with the real problem this lesson is about: pricing pages change.

Picture opening the worksheet six months from now. You see "web search: $14 per 1,000 — typed by Sam." You still can't tell where $14 came from. Was it the list price, or your company's deal? Which region? Is it still true? You'd have to find Sam. Sam may not remember, or may have left the company.

A name points to a person. What you need is a way to check the number yourself and to know how old it is. A price is only true on a certain page, on a certain day. When the page updates, an old number quietly goes stale, and your estimates go wrong without anyone noticing.

"The page it came from, and the date" is the right answer because anyone can open that page, check the price, see if it has changed since that date, and update the line.

check:0:2.q: Why not “A note saying prices never change”?
check:0:2.a:
**"A note saying prices never change"** has one good instinct. It tries to tell the reader how far to trust the number. That part is fair. A bare "$14 per 1,000" leaves people guessing.

But the note says something false. The lesson's first point is that pricing pages change. Providers raise prices, cut them, rename tiers, and add regions. A note promising the price is fixed would mislead the next reader. They might keep using an old number long after it stopped being true.

It also gives them nothing to act on. If the price looks wrong, where do they look? The note doesn't say. And if the bill comes in at three times the plan, nobody can quickly tell whether the price moved or the usage did.

The right answer is **"The page it came from, and the date."** It lets anyone open the same page, see whether it changed since that day, and update the line. For example:

```
# web search: $14 per 1,000 (provider's pricing page, checked 2025-03-01)
```

check:1:1.q: Why not “One region is always faster”?
check:1:1.a:
"One region is always faster" is not the best answer because it rests on a claim the lesson never makes. The lesson talks about price, units, and what you really pay. It says nothing about speed. And the word "always" is risky. Very few things in cloud pricing are "always" true.

What it gets right: it sees that picking a region can be about more than the price tag. A **region** is one area of data centers, like US East. A **Global deployment** is a different pricing tier from a single-region one. Here, the region costs $0.022 instead of $0.02, so something has to make that extra 10% worth paying.

What it misses: a good reason to pay more is a firm rule your project must follow. "It might be quicker" is not a firm rule. You would have to measure it before relying on it.

"Your data must stay in that region" is better because it is a hard requirement, often set by law or company policy. When a requirement like that applies, the slightly higher price is simply the cost of following the rule.

judge.notes: No real problems. The closing explanation runs to two sentences where one was asked for, which is minor.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Global prices change every day”?
check:1:2.a:
"Global prices change every day" sounds reasonable, because the lesson does say pricing pages change. That's why you write down the source and the date next to each price.

But this answer misses the point of the question in two ways.

First, the question gives you two fixed prices: $0.02 per million tokens for Global and $0.022 for one region. Global is the cheaper one. Saying its price might move doesn't explain why you'd choose to pay more.

Second, the lesson never says one kind of price changes more than another. Both prices come from pricing pages, and any page can change. So "prices change" applies to the region price too. It isn't a reason to pick one over the other.

The question is really about something cost can't settle. Sometimes a rule matters more than saving two tenths of a cent. A "rule" here could be a law, a contract, or your company's policy about where data is handled.

"Your data must stay in that region" is better because it gives a real requirement that can make the slightly higher price the right choice.

check:2:1.a:
The pricing calculator is a good tool, just for a different moment. It helps you **plan**. You type in what you expect to use, and it multiplies that by the list price. That is useful before launch, when you have no bill yet.

But the question asks what your feature **really cost last month**. The calculator can't answer that, for two reasons:

- **It doesn't know what you used.** It only knows what you typed in. If web search ran three times more than planned, the calculator still shows the plan.
- **It shows the list price.** That is the public price for one region and the standard tier. Your company may pay a different rate through its agreement.

So the calculator gives you an estimate. The question wants the real number.

`system.billing.usage` is a built-in Databricks table, which works like a spreadsheet Databricks fills in for you. It records the DBUs (Databricks Units, the measure Databricks bills by) your workloads actually used, day by day.

`system.billing.usage` is better because it shows what you actually used last month, not what you guessed you would use.

judge.notes: No major problem. The only minor point is that 'day by day' and 'built-in' for system.billing.usage go beyond what the lesson states, but they do not contradict it.

check:2:2.a:
The model's documentation is a fair guess. It tells you what the model does. It may even list a price per unit, like dollars per million tokens. That helps you **plan** a cost before launch.

But the question asks what your feature **really cost last month**. The documentation can't answer that. It doesn't know:

- How many tokens or DBUs (Databricks Units, the measure Databricks bills by) your feature actually used.
- Whether usage spiked, like the web search line that came in at 3 times the plan.
- Your company's own rate, region or tier. Docs show list prices at best.

So the documentation gives you an estimate. It never gives you a bill.

`system.billing.usage` is a system table. That is a table Databricks fills in for you automatically. It records the DBUs your workspace actually used, broken down by day and by what used them. Multiply those DBUs by your company's price for one DBU and you get real dollars.

**In one sentence:** `system.billing.usage` is better because it shows what you actually used, not what you expected to use.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Price per unit, times the units one task uses” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "Providers bill in different units. Models charge per million tokens. Search charges per 1,000 searches. Databricks charges per DBU. You can't budget until they all share one unit."

*The idea.* "So I price one finished task. For each thing it uses, I divide the price by the unit size. Then I multiply by how much one task uses, and add the lines up. Say a model costs $2 per million input tokens. One task sends 1,800 tokens in, so that line costs $0.0036."

*The edge case.* "A pricing page shows a list price, for one region and one tier. My company's rate may differ. So I write the source and date beside each line. After launch, I check it against the real bill."

Jargon: *tokens* are small chunks of text a model reads or writes. A *DBU* (Databricks Unit) is the unit Databricks bills by.

**A likely follow-up**

"The bill came in three times your estimate. What do you do?"

Hint: don't just raise the budget. Find which line drifted. Then check the traces, which are records of each step a task took. Maybe the agent calls web search more often than you planned.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The estimate is off by a round factor, like 1,000 or 1,000,000.** This usually means a unit was misread. For example, a price "per million tokens" was treated as "per thousand." A task you planned at $0.0036 shows up as $3.60.
- **Every line of the bill is lower than planned by about the same percent.** You probably used the list price, and your company's agreement gives a discount. A different region or currency can also shift every line.
- **One line is far above plan**, like web search at 3 times the estimate. Each task likely uses more units than you assumed, such as two searches instead of half of one. Traces show this. A trace is the step-by-step record of what your agent did.
- **A price has no source or date next to it.** You can't tell if it is out of date, because pricing pages change.

**Quickest check**

Pick one line. Open its pricing page, read the unit, and redo the sum by hand. Then compare one day of real spend with your estimate times the number of tasks run that day. On Azure, use Azure Cost Management. On Databricks, use the `system.billing.usage` table.

judge.notes: Minor: it assumes the company agreement means a discount (the lesson only says the rate differs), and its 'two searches instead of half' example would be 4 times the plan, not the 3 times it mentions.

learn:stops.a:
**1. Each task uses a different amount.** The method assumes one task uses a fixed amount, like 1,800 input tokens and half a search. Agents don't always behave that way. One task might loop or call web search five times. Estimate from an average, then check traces (the step-by-step logs of what the agent did) to see the real spread.

**2. Your price isn't the list price.** The page shows one region, the standard tier and no discounts. You might pay a different rate through your company's agreement, region or currency. A Batch, Global or reserved option can also change the price. The DBU price also differs by product and region, since $0.07 is for model serving in US East. Ask whoever buys cloud services at your company for your actual rate.

**3. The page changes, or the estimate drifts.** Prices go stale. Usage can also grow in ways you didn't plan. Keep the source and date next to every line, and recheck them. After launch, compare against the real bill in Azure Cost Management or the `system.billing.usage` table. Look into anything far off plan.

judge.notes: No real problems. Minor: each point runs 5-6 sentences against the 2-3 sentence guidance, and the claim that DBU prices differ by product and region goes slightly beyond the lesson, though it follows from the '$0.07 for model serving in US East' wording.

learn:term.a:
Every cost estimate you make is only as good as the price you started from. Prices sit on provider pages, and those pages change. If you skip reading the unit, or forget where a number came from, small mistakes turn into big bills.

Here is a realistic case. A team plans an agent that searches the web. Someone sees "$14" and reads it as $14 for 1,000 tokens (tokens are the small chunks of text a model reads). It was really $14 per 1,000 searches. The plan says $210 a month. Each task also runs more searches than they guessed. The real bill comes in at $630. Nobody knows where the $210 came from, so nobody can tell which part was wrong.

The four habits prevent this:

- Read the unit, so "per 1,000 searches" never gets mixed up with "per million tokens."
- Price one task, so the estimate matches how the agent really works.
- Write the source and date, so anyone can check it later.
- Compare against the real bill after launch, so a 3-times gap gets caught early.

judge.notes: The example is a bit muddled: it blames a unit misread, then says the gap came from extra searches per task. Nothing in it contradicts the lesson, though.

check:0:0.q: Why not “Ask Claude in the instructions to add up the co…”?
check:0:0.a:
Asking Claude to "add up the costs carefully" gets one thing right. It puts the requirement in the instructions, so Claude knows a total is needed. That part is good.

What it misses is that the word "carefully" doesn't change how Claude works. Claude is a language model. It writes answers by predicting likely text, not by doing exact arithmetic the way a calculator does. Most of the time the sum will be right. Sometimes a number will be slightly off, and it may come out different on two runs with the same inputs. You can't easily tell which runs went wrong.

The total cost of ownership (every cost of running the idea over time, added up) is exactly the kind of figure people make decisions on. One wrong digit there matters.

That is why this skill ships with `scripts/tco.py`. Claude passes it the inputs, the script does the maths, and Claude reports the table it prints.

**Why the script wins:** a script gives the same correct total every time for the same inputs, and you can test it once and trust it.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Write the current prices into the description”?
check:0:2.a:
Putting prices into the description has one good instinct: real numbers are better than guesses. But it puts them in the wrong place and still leaves the hard part undone.

First, the description has a different job. Claude reads the name and description of every skill up front to decide *whether* to use it. It is a short "what this does and when to use it" note, capped at 1,024 characters. A price list there crowds out the words that help Claude pick your skill at the right moment.

Second, it doesn't make the answer reliable. Even with the right prices, Claude would still add up the total cost of ownership (all the costs of running the system over time) in its head. A model can get sums wrong.

Third, prices change. Numbers baked into a description go stale quietly.

The right answer is better because a script like `scripts/tco.py` does the arithmetic the same way every time, so the total is exact, and the skill just runs it and reports the table.

check:1:0.q: Why not “The script that adds up costs”?
check:1:0.a:
The cost script is a sensible thing to check, just not first. It is the right place for exact sums, because a model can add numbers wrong and a script cannot. If your cost table came out wrong, `scripts/tco.py` would be the first suspect.

But look at the problem. Claude never uses the skill at all. The script only runs at step 8, after Claude has already picked the skill and started following its steps. So the script never gets a chance to run. Fixing it cannot change whether the skill is chosen.

Here is how choosing works. Up front, Claude reads only the `name` and `description` of every skill. It loads the rest of `SKILL.md` only when a request matches. If the `description` never says something like "Use when someone asks whether an AI idea is worth doing", Claude has no reason to pick it.

"The description: when to use it" is better because, of the two settings Claude reads before choosing, the `description` is the one that says when the skill applies, so it decides whether the skill is ever used.

check:1:1.q: Why not “The output format at the end”?
check:1:1.a:
The output format is a real part of a good skill. It tells Claude what the finished answer should look like, such as the cost table and a clear verdict. If that part were vague, you would get messy or uneven results.

But that only matters once the skill is running. The problem here comes earlier: Claude never uses the skill at all.

Remember how Claude finds skills. Up front, it reads only two things from every skill: the `name` and the `description` in the frontmatter (the settings between the `---` markers). The body, including the output format, loads only after a request matches. So Claude never even sees the output format until it has already picked the skill. Fixing it cannot help Claude pick it.

The `description: when to use it` is the better answer. The name is mostly a label, so the description is what Claude compares against your request. It must say what the skill does and when to use it, for example "Use when someone asks whether an AI idea is worth doing."

judge.notes: Minor: 'a clear verdict' and 'the name is mostly a label' go slightly beyond the lesson, but neither contradicts it.

check:2:0.a:
Putting the folder in `~/.claude/skills/` does work. Claude Code will find the skill and load it. The catch is who gets it.

The `~` symbol is short for your home folder. That is the personal space on your own computer, for example `/Users/sam` or `C:\Users\sam`. Skills kept there are for you alone. They follow you into every project you open, but they never leave your machine.

Your teammates have their own home folders, so they would not see your skill. Each of them would have to copy the folder over by hand. Then, when you improve the instructions, their copies would fall out of date.

A project's `.claude/skills/` folder sits inside the project's repository. A repository is the shared set of files the team keeps in version control, a tool like Git that tracks changes and lets everyone download the latest copy. You commit the skill (save it into the repository's history). After that, anyone who pulls the project gets the same skill, including every later fix.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Check the rules, then write the file” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* A Claude skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file. Claude reads its name and description first. If those break the rules, the skill will not load.

*The idea.* So I check before I write. I gather every rule the input breaks and report them all together. Only when nothing is wrong do I build the file. That means the frontmatter (the settings between `---` markers), then a title, then numbered steps. It's like a form that is checked before it is sent.

*The trade-off.* Collecting every problem takes a little more code than stopping at the first one. But the person can fix everything in one pass instead of retrying again and again.

**Likely follow-up:** "Why not just write the file and fix problems later?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Catching mistakes when the file is created is cheaper than finding out later that the skill would not load. You could add that passing the rules isn't the whole job. learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs your skill is broken or never ran**

- **It never kicks in.** You ask Claude to assess an AI idea, and it answers in its own loose way. There is no one-line use case, no gates, no cost table. Usually the description is too vague. Or the file broke a rule, so Claude never saw the skill at all.
- **The answers drift.** Two similar ideas come back in different shapes, with steps missing or reordered. A skill is meant to make the routine identical every time.
- **The cost totals wobble.** The same inputs give slightly different totals, or the rows don't add up. That means the model did the sums itself instead of running `scripts/tco.py`.
- **Known gaps slip through.** You feed it an idea with an obvious hole, like no acceptance criteria, and it passes anyway.

**Quickest check**

Open a fresh Claude Code session and type `/vet-ai-use-case`. If it isn't offered, the skill didn't load, so recheck the frontmatter (the settings between the `---` markers). If it loads, run one idea whose gaps you already know. Then compare its cost table with what `tco.py` prints when you run it yourself on the same inputs.

learn:stops.a:
**1. The description is vague or overlaps another skill.** Claude reads only the name and description up front, so a fuzzy description means your skill never loads, or a similar one loads instead. Name the exact trigger, like "when someone asks whether an AI idea is worth doing," and test it with real requests.

**2. The facts behind the routine change over time.** Prices, approved models and company rules shift, and a skill written once quietly goes out of date. Keep changing numbers in a separate reference file or in the inputs the script reads. Then review the skill on a schedule.

**3. The routine grows very large.** A huge SKILL.md is slow to load and hard for Claude to follow, and different teams may vet ideas differently. Keep the main steps short. Move details into reference files that Claude opens only when needed, or split the routine into several smaller skills.

In every case, test it the same way the lesson says. Run the skill on ideas with known problems, see what it misses, and fix the instructions.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Uses times the price per thousand” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

**The problem:** Some tools don't charge by tokens (the chunks of text a model reads and writes). Web search and document reading charge per use. Those bills can be bigger than the model's own bill.

**The idea:** Count the uses, multiply by the price per 1,000, then divide by 1,000. Say 30,000 questions a month each search once, at $14 per 1,000 searches. That's 30,000 times 14 divided by 1,000, so $420 a month.

**The edge case:** Agents multiply it. An agent may search three times for one question. That's 90,000 searches, or $1,260 a month, which is triple the $420. So I take the calls per question from traces (logs of the steps in real runs), not from guesses.

**A likely follow-up**

*"How would you cut that bill?"*

Hint: Use the cheapest service that does the job, and do the work once.

- Read each document once, when it arrives, not again for every question.
- Use plain text reading at $1.50 per 1,000 pages instead of layout at $10 when you don't need tables.
- Cap the number of searches per task.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The bill beats your estimate.** You planned for model tokens only. Then the invoice shows search or document reading costing more than the model itself.
- **Costs grow faster than usage.** Questions went up 10%, but the search bill doubled. That often means the agent is calling search more times per question than you assumed.
- **Pages billed exceed pages owned.** You have 20,000 pages of documents, but the invoice shows far more. Something is re-reading the same documents on every question instead of once, when they arrive.
- **The pricey option everywhere.** Every page goes through Layout at $10 per 1,000, even plain text that needs no tables. The $1.50 Read option would do.

**Quickest check**

Open a sample of your traces. A trace is the step-by-step record of what the agent did for one question. Count the tool calls in each and take the average per question. Multiply by your monthly questions and the price per 1,000, then divide by 1,000. If that is far below the invoice, your assumptions are off. Then look for loops, or for searches with no cap.

learn:stops.a:
The simple sum (uses times price, divided by 1,000) works well until one of these shows up.

**Agents with wildly varying call counts.** An average of "2 searches per question" from your traces can hide a few questions where the agent loops and searches 20 times. A trace is the log of each step an agent took. Budget for the heavy cases, not just the average, and put a hard cap on calls per task so a loop can't run up the bill.

**Prices that aren't flat.** Real price lists often have free allowances, volume discounts, or a different price above a certain amount. "Page" can also mean something unexpected, such as a fixed number of characters for some file types. Read the pricing page and work out each price band separately.

**Usage that changes over time.** "Read each document once" stops being once if you later switch to a better model and reprocess everything. It also grows as new documents arrive. Count reprocessing as a fresh one-off cost, and rerun the sum each month with current traces.

judge.notes: No problems. The pricing-page points (free allowances, discounts, what counts as a page) go beyond the lesson but do not contradict it.

learn:term.a:
Most cost planning focuses on tokens, the small chunks of text a model reads and writes. Tools work differently. They charge a flat price **each time** you use them, and that can quietly grow bigger than the model bill.

Here is how it goes wrong. A team builds the HR assistant. They plan for 30,000 questions a month and guess "one web search per question." That's $420 a month, so they budget for it.

Then the agent goes live. Agents decide for themselves when to call a tool, and this one often searches three times to feel sure. Nobody checked the traces, which are the logs of each step the agent took. The real bill is $1,260 a month. That's three times the plan, with no change to the model at all.

The same thing happens with documents. If the agent re-reads 20,000 pages with the $10 layout service on every question, a one-time $200 job becomes a cost you pay on every question.

Counting uses, not just tokens, lets you spot this before the invoice does. Then you can cap searches, read documents once, and pick the cheapest service that works.

What it misses is what break-even means. Break-even is the number of tasks a month you need just to cover the fixed monthly costs (search, logging, monitoring). Below that line, the savings don't even pay the running bills. Nothing is left over to pay back the build.

Here's an example with numbers that fit the question. Say each task saves $5 and fixed costs are $10,000 a month. Then break-even is $10,000 ÷ $5 = 2,000 tasks.

- At 1,500 tasks: 1,500 × $5 = $7,500 saved.
- Minus $10,000 fixed = **−$2,500 a month**.

So the monthly net is below zero. "Slower payback" would need a smaller *positive* net. A negative net means each month digs the hole deeper. That's why payback has no answer here, and the lesson's code returns `None`, Python's word for no value.

"It loses money every month, so the build never pays back" is better because it sees that falling below break-even makes the monthly net negative, not just smaller.

But it draws the wrong conclusion from that. Leaving out the build doesn't make things safer. It means break-even is the *easiest* bar to clear. If you can't clear it, you're in trouble before the build even comes up.

Here's a quick picture. Say break-even is 2,000 tasks because fixed costs are $10,000 a month and each task saves $5. At 1,500 tasks, you save $7,500. You still pay $10,000. So the **monthly net** (savings minus fixed costs) is minus $2,500. You lose money every single month.

With a negative monthly net, there's nothing to pay the build back with. **Payback** (build cost divided by monthly net) has no sensible answer. That's why the lesson says payback is `None` in that case.

"It loses money every month, so the build never pays back" is better because it reads falling short of break-even correctly. Running costs aren't covered, so the build can't be recovered either.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Check before you divide” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* "A task can save money every time and still lose money overall. Running costs come every month, and the build has to be paid back. Payback months is the build cost divided by the monthly net. If the monthly net is zero, Python crashes on the divide. If it's negative, you get negative months, which looks like an answer but means nothing."

*The idea:* "So I work out the monthly net first: saving per task times tasks a month, minus fixed costs. I only divide if that net is above zero. If it isn't, I report 'no payback' instead of a fake number."

*The edge case:* "The trade-off is that 'no payback' isn't a number. Whatever reads the result has to handle that case, or a chart or report could break later."

**A likely follow-up**

*"Break-even divides too. What could go wrong there?"*

Hint for a strong answer: break-even is fixed costs divided by saving per task. If the saving per task is zero or negative, no number of tasks ever covers the running costs. So the same habit applies: check what you're dividing by before you divide.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs the math was skipped or done wrong**

- **Payback comes out negative.** That means the monthly net was below zero and someone divided anyway. A negative number of months is nonsense. It really means "never pays back."
- **Payback is huge, like 80 months.** The net is barely above zero. A small dip in volume and it flips to a loss.
- **Real tasks a month sit close to break-even.** If break-even is 1,775 and you only see 2,000 tickets, you have almost no cushion.
- **The case looked great, then the savings never show up in the budget.** Often the "saving" was soft, like quieter afternoons. Nobody hired fewer people.
- **Saving per task ignores uncaught mistakes.** The numbers look rosy until mistakes found later start costing money.
- **The MLflow run still logs the original guesses.** Nobody swapped them for numbers the POC (proof of concept, the small trial build) actually measured.

**Quickest check**

Take the measured tasks a month from the POC. Compare it to break-even. Then redo the monthly net by hand. If it isn't comfortably above zero, the business case doesn't hold.

judge.notes: Minor: the 80-month bullet blames a barely positive net, but a very large build cost could also cause a long payback. Otherwise it fits the lesson.

learn:stops.a:
The simple rule assumes every month looks the same. Here are three places where that breaks.

**Usage ramps up slowly.** Staff rarely switch over on day one. Early months might see 1,000 tickets, not 6,000, so real payback takes longer than build cost divided by monthly net. Plan month by month with a ramp, and track actual volume during the POC (proof of concept, the small trial build).

**Quality or prices drift.** With an LLM app, costs per task shift when the model provider changes prices or prompts grow longer. Mistakes can also creep up as policies or documents change, which raises the "mistakes nobody caught" cost. Re-measure saving per task regularly, for example by logging new MLflow runs, and redo the numbers.

**Costs jump at scale.** "Fixed" costs often stay flat only up to a point. Past it, you may need a bigger search index or more monitoring staff, so costs step up suddenly. Work out break-even separately for each cost level.

Also, if the savings are only soft (quieter afternoons, not real money), no payback ever arrives.

learn:term.q: How is “hard saving” different from “soft saving”?
learn:term.a:
Both come from the same thing: staff spending less time on a task. The difference is whether that freed time turns into real money.

A **hard saving** shows up in the budget. In the lesson's words: fewer new hires or less overtime. Money that would have been spent is now not spent.

A **soft saving** is time freed up that doesn't change any bill. People have quieter afternoons, but the company pays the same wages as before.

An everyday comparison: you buy a dishwasher. If it lets you cancel the cleaner you pay each week, that's a hard saving. If it just gives you a calmer evening, that's a soft saving. Nice, but your bank balance is the same.

How they work together: the lesson has the business owner confirm which kind the staff time saved really is. That check comes before you trust the numbers.

In the HR example, the saving per ticket is about $5.64. Times 6,000 tickets, that drives the monthly net and the 6.3-month payback. Those numbers only describe real money if the owner confirms the time saved is a hard saving.
