check:0:2.a:
This option gets one thing right. It notices that the trouble is tied to a time of day. The errors come every morning, so something about mornings matters.

But it blames the wrong thing. The tokens-per-minute limit (the most tokens your deployment may use in one minute) is a fixed number set by the platform team. It does not shrink in the morning. Price also has nothing to do with error 429. Cost is what you pay for tokens. The limit is how many tokens a minute you are allowed. These are separate things.

What really happens in the morning is a rush. Many users arrive at once, so the busiest minute carries far more tokens than an average minute. The daily average hides that rush because it spreads the traffic evenly across the whole day. The limit stays the same, but the demand jumps over it, and the model or the gateway sends back "too many requests".

"It was sized from the daily average, not the busiest minute" is better because it names the real cause: the limit was set too low for the morning peak.

judge.notes: No serious problems. The closing sentence is a little loose: it says the limit was 'set too low' rather than that the plan was sized from the daily average, and the answer runs close to 200 words.

check:1:0.a:
The daily token total isn't useless. It tells you how much work the system does in a day, which helps with things like cost. So it's a real number worth knowing.

But it doesn't answer this question. The limits that cause error 429 ("too many requests") are counted **per minute**, not per day. A daily total spreads the work evenly across the hours. That hides the busy minutes, which is exactly the mistake this lesson warns about. You've also already checked the busiest minute against the deployment's quota (the most tokens a minute that one copy of the model may use). Looking at the daily total adds nothing new about whether users will hit 429.

What it misses is the second limit on the path. Every request passes through the **gateway**, the front door in front of the model. The gateway has its own **rate limits**, meaning caps on how much it lets through each minute. Your busiest minute could fit the model's quota and still be blocked at the gateway.

"The gateway's rate limits too" is better because it checks the other per-minute limit that can also send back error 429.

check:1:2.q: Why not “Nothing: that's the only limit”?
check:1:2.a:
"Nothing: that's the only limit" gets one thing right. Checking the Foundry deployment's quota is a real and necessary step. A **quota** is the most tokens per minute that one **deployment** (your copy of the model) may use. If your busiest minute fits under it, the model itself won't turn you away.

But the model is not the only limit. Every request first passes through the **gateway**, the front door between your app and the model. The gateway has its own **rate limits**, which cap how much it lets through each minute. Those limits are set separately, often by the platform team. They can be lower than the deployment's quota.

So your busiest minute could fit the model's quota and still go over the gateway's limit. Users would still see error 429, "too many requests". It doesn't matter which limit sent it. To the user, it's the same failure.

Think of it as two doors in a row. You need to fit through both.

"The gateway's rate limits too" is better because it checks every limit on the request's path, and either one can send back a 429.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Each task is sent three times”?
check:2:0.a:
"Each task is sent three times" gets one thing right. Multiplying by 3 does triple the tokens you plan for. But it gives the wrong reason for doing it.

The burst factor is not about repeats. Each task is still counted once. The factor is about *timing*. Even inside the busiest hour, tasks don't arrive evenly, one neat batch per minute. They bunch up. A few minutes get a rush, and others are quiet.

Your average for that hour hides those rushes. The burst factor is your guess at how much busier the busiest minute is than an average minute of that hour. 3 is a fair first guess. The POC (proof of concept, your small trial run) then checks it against real 1-minute peaks.

If tasks really were sent three times, that extra traffic would use up the limit too. But that is a separate question from the one the burst factor answers.

"Some minutes are far busier than others" is better because it names the real reason: traffic comes in bursts, and the limit is counted per minute, so you must size for the busiest one.

check:2:1.q: Why not “To leave room for three models”?
check:2:1.a:
The option "To leave room for three models" gets one thing half right. Multiplying by 3 does make your number bigger, so you end up with spare room. But the reason for that room has nothing to do with how many models you run.

The 3 is not a count of anything. It is the **burst factor**: how much busier the busiest single minute is than an average minute of the busiest hour. Within that hour, tasks don't arrive in a smooth stream. They bunch up. One minute might get 3 tickets while the next gets none. The 3 is just a fair first guess for how big that bunching is. Your POC (proof of concept, the small trial version) can measure the real value from 1-minute peaks. It might turn out to be 2 or 5.

If you ran three models, that would change where traffic goes. It would not change how unevenly it arrives.

"Some minutes are far busier than others" is better because it names the real reason: traffic bunches up within the hour, and the tokens-per-minute limit is checked minute by minute.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Size for the busiest minute, not the day” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
The limit is checked minute by minute, or even faster. It never looks at your whole day. So a day that looks fine on average can still break.

Requests bunch up. Many arrive in one busy hour, and inside that hour they come in bursts. A burst is a short spell when far more requests arrive than usual.

Here is what goes wrong. Say you pick a **quota** from the daily average. A quota is the most tokens a minute your model deployment may use. Quiet minutes pass fine. Then the rush hits, the busiest minute goes over the limit, and users get error 429, "too many requests". The bot fails exactly when the most people need it.

A small example: 270 HR tickets a day, 25,000 tokens each. Spread evenly over 8 hours, that is about 14,000 tokens a minute. Now say a fifth of the tickets land in one hour, and the busiest minute is 3 times busier than that hour's average. That minute needs about 67,500 tokens, almost 5 times the average.

So start from the busiest hour and multiply by a burst factor. Then compare the result with the deployment's tokens-per-minute limit. Check the gateway's limit too.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Daily count to busiest minute” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem:* "Traffic is never even through the day. If I size from the daily average, the busiest minute goes over the model's tokens-per-minute limit. Then users get error 429, 'too many requests'."

*The idea:* "So I size for the busiest minute. I take tasks a day, keep the share that lands in the busiest hour, and divide by 60. I multiply by a burst factor, often 3 to start, for spikes inside that hour. Then I multiply by the tokens each task asks for: the prompt plus the longest answer allowed."

*The trade-off:* "Sizing for the peak means paying for room you rarely use. But running short means failed requests at the worst moment, like a café understaffed at lunch."

**A likely follow-up**

"Where do those numbers come from?"

Hint: the business owner gives tasks a day. A proof of concept (POC, a small trial run) measures the busy hour, the burst, and tokens per task. The platform team gives the deployment quota (the most one model copy may use) and the gateway limits (caps at the front door every request passes through). Add that either limit can return 429.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**The warning signs**

The clearest sign is error 429, "too many requests", showing up in your logs in clumps. It comes at busy times, like Monday morning, and is quiet the rest of the day. Your daily or hourly charts look calm and well under the limit. That mismatch is the clue: someone sized from the average.

Other signs:
- Users report slow answers or failures at the same times each day. Your app may be quietly retrying after each 429.
- A test with smooth, even traffic passed. Real traffic still fails, because real traffic comes in bursts.
- You hit the limit even though the tokens you actually used look lower. That happens because the quota counts the prompt plus the longest answer allowed (`max_tokens`), not what was used.

**The quickest check**

Look up the busiest few minutes from last week in the gateway's usage table. Add room on top, because that table shows tokens used, not tokens asked for. Then compare against both limits: the deployment's tokens-per-minute quota and the gateway's rate limits. Also check which of the two sent the 429s. That tells you which limit to raise.

learn:stops.a:
**1. The busy times change.** A company-wide announcement or month-end payroll can push far more tickets into one hour than the POC (proof of concept, the small trial version) ever saw. A burst factor of 3 may then be too low. Re-run the usage-table query every few weeks, plan for the worst real minute plus spare room, and grow the quota as use grows.

**2. One task makes several model calls.** Some apps call the model more than once per ticket. For example, they draft an answer, check it, then rewrite it. Each extra call adds its own prompt and answer, so tokens per task can be two or three times what you expected. Count the tokens across every call one task might make in the worst case, not just the first call.

**3. Other apps share your limits.** Your deployment's quota or the gateway's rate limits may be shared with other teams. Your busiest minute can fit by itself, yet still hit error 429 when their busiest minute lands at the same time. Ask the platform team who else shares those limits. Then check that everyone's peaks added together still fit.

judge.notes: Items 2 and 3 each run to four sentences, over the two-or-three limit, but the content is consistent with the lesson and all five checks pass.

learn:term.a:
They're closely linked, but they aren't the same thing.

**To size** a system is to decide one number: how many tokens a minute it must handle. It answers "how big?"

**Capacity planning** is doing that sizing *ahead of time*, as part of a bigger job. You gather the inputs, work out the size, and then check it against the limits on the path. Those are the deployment's quota and the gateway's rate limits. That way, nothing breaks after launch.

So sizing is one step. Capacity planning is the whole habit of doing that step early and acting on it.

**Everyday comparison:** a café owner decides "we need 4 staff for the lunch rush." That's sizing. Working this out the week before opening, then checking the budget and the rota, is capacity planning.

**In the lesson's example:** working out that the busiest minute needs about 75000 tokens is sizing. Doing it before go-live, then asking the platform team for a quota above 75000, is capacity planning. It also means checking the gateway limits too, so users don't hit error 429.

check:0:1.a:
Your math is right. 42,000 divided by 3,000 really is 14. So "14" is exactly how much capacity your busiest minute needs.

The catch is that the deployment won't accept 14. A deployment is the copy of the model you set up and pay for. For `gpt-4.1` on Global, the smallest deployment you can create is 15 PTUs. A PTU (provisioned throughput unit) is one block of model capacity kept just for you. You can't order fewer than the minimum, even if your app would never use the extra one.

Think of buying eggs by the box. You might need 14 eggs, but if the smallest box holds 15, you walk out with 15. Capacity is sold in whole blocks, not in any amount you like.

That extra PTU isn't wasted, either. It gives you a little headroom, meaning spare room, so a minute slightly busier than you expected still fits.

"15" is better because it is the smallest amount you can actually buy that still covers your busiest minute.

check:0:2.a:
"42" starts from the right number. 42,000 tokens a minute is the correct busiest-minute load, with output already weighted. But "42" just drops the thousands. It never divides by what one PTU handles.

A PTU (provisioned throughput unit) is one block of model capacity kept just for you. Here each one handles 3,000 tokens a minute. So the real sum is 42,000 divided by 3,000, which gives 14 PTUs, not 42.

Then there's one more step. A deployment has a minimum size. For `gpt-4.1` on Global, that's 15 PTUs. 14 is under the minimum, so you round up to 15. It's like eggs sold in boxes: you can't buy 14 if the smallest box holds 15.

Buying 42 would also be costly. Reserved monthly, that's 42 × $260 = $10,920. The right size costs 15 × $260 = $3,900. You'd pay nearly three times as much for capacity you never use.

"15" is better because it divides the load by one PTU's capacity, then rounds up to the deployment's minimum.

check:1:1.q: Why not “Nothing, because it was idle”?
check:1:1.a:
"Nothing, because it was idle" mixes up the two ways to pay.

**What it gets right:** that is exactly how pay per token works. With the Standard option, you pay for each token (a small chunk of text) the model reads or writes. No requests all weekend means no tokens, so no bill.

**What it misses:** a PTU (provisioned throughput unit) works differently. You are renting a block of model capacity that is kept just for you. That capacity sits ready every hour, so you pay for every hour, whether you use it or not. The lesson also notes that billing can't be paused. It runs until you delete the deployment. Reserved monthly terms are billed in full too.

For example, 15 PTUs on Global at $1.00 an hour, idle for a 48-hour weekend, still costs 15 × $1.00 × 48 = $720.

Think of it like renting a parking space. You pay for the space even when your car isn't in it.

"The full hourly price" is better because PTUs charge for capacity that is held for you, not for the work you actually do.

check:1:2.a:
"Half the hourly price" gets one thing right. You do still pay something over the weekend, even though nothing is running. So it avoids the trap of thinking idle hours are free.

But it assumes the price drops when the deployment (your set-up copy of the model) sits idle. That isn't how a PTU works.

A PTU is capacity kept just for you. Nobody else can use it, whether you send a request or not. So you are paying for the reservation itself, not for the work done. Busy hour, quiet hour, or empty weekend, each hour costs the same.

The lesson also says billing can't be paused. It keeps running until you delete the deployment. There is no "idle rate" and no half-price mode.

This is the real difference from pay per token. With pay per token, an empty weekend costs nothing, because you only pay for tokens (small chunks of text) used.

"The full hourly price" is better because a PTU charges every hour for capacity held for you, used or not, until the deployment is deleted.

check:2:1.a:
"They fail with error 429" describes what happens **without** spillover. That part is real. Error 429 means "too many requests." The service is saying it has no room for you right now. A full PTU deployment with nothing behind it will send that error back.

But the question says spillover is **on**. Spillover exists to stop exactly that failure. When your reserved capacity is full, spillover sends the extra requests somewhere else instead of turning them away.

That "somewhere else" is a pay-per-token deployment. It is the Standard kind, where you pay for each token used. So the extra requests still get answered. You pay for them by the token, on top of your hourly PTU bill.

So the 429 answer misses the whole point of the setting. It treats spillover as if it did nothing.

"They go to a pay-per-token deployment" is better because it describes what spillover actually does: it moves the overflow to Standard capacity, so the requests are served instead of failing.

judge.notes: No real problems. The claim that a full PTU deployment returns 429 isn't stated in the lesson, but it fits the lesson's 'instead of failing' and is true.

check:2:2.q: Why not “They wait for the next hour”?
check:2:2.a:
It's an easy mix-up, because the lesson does mention hours. A PTU deployment is billed by the hour. That part is true. But billing is about how you pay. It doesn't control what happens to your requests.

Here's what the answer misses. Capacity is sized per minute, from the busiest minute. When that minute's capacity is full, nothing in the setup holds extra requests for an hour. A user waiting an hour for a reply would be a broken app anyway.

**Spillover** exists for exactly this moment. It's a setting that sends the extra requests somewhere else when the PTU deployment is full. That somewhere is a pay-per-token deployment, which is a second deployment that charges for each token used. So the request still gets answered right away. You just pay for its tokens at the normal per-token price, instead of the request failing.

"They go to a pay-per-token deployment" is better because that is exactly what spillover does: it moves the overflow to pay-per-token so the extra requests are served now, not delayed or dropped.

judge.notes: No significant problems. Minor: 'right away' and 'normal per-token price' go slightly beyond the lesson's wording, and 'PTU' is not re-explained.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Normalize, divide, then round up to the minimum…” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem.* With pay per token, a busy minute can hit error 429, meaning "too many requests." A PTU (provisioned throughput unit) is model capacity kept just for you. The question is how many to buy.

*The idea.* Size from the busiest minute. First, normalize: convert everything into input tokens. For gpt-4.1, one output token counts as 4 input tokens. So 30,000 input plus 3,000 output becomes 42,000. Next, divide by what one PTU handles, which is 3,000 a minute. That gives 14.

*The edge case.* Capacity is sold in whole blocks. On Global, gpt-4.1 needs at least 15 PTUs, then steps of 5. So 14 becomes 15. It's like eggs: the smallest box holds 15.

**A likely follow-up**

"Will PTUs save us money?"

Hint: say no. They buy capacity, not savings. For a load this busy all month, pay per token is about $3,679. Reserved PTUs cost $3,900, and hourly PTUs cost $10,950. What you pay for is steady speed. Then mention spillover. If the PTU deployment is full, extra requests go to pay per token instead of failing.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that the PTU sizing went wrong**

A **PTU** (provisioned throughput unit) is a block of model capacity kept just for you. Here is what a slip looks like in your numbers.

- **The count is suspiciously low.** Output tokens were counted the same as input tokens. Or the size came from an average minute instead of the busiest one.
- **The count isn't a size you can buy.** It has a fraction, like 14.3. It sits below the deployment's minimum. Or it falls between steps, like 17 on Global or 60 on Regional.
- **The budget expected savings.** Someone thought PTUs would cost less than pay per token. The lesson's example shows they cost about the same or more, even when busy all month.
- **The bill keeps running.** Someone assumed a deployment could be paused. It can't. Billing runs until it is deleted.
- **Requests fail when the PTU deployment is full.** **Spillover** was left off. Spillover sends extra requests to a pay-per-token deployment instead.

**Quickest check:** Run the lesson's worked example (30,000 input, 3,000 output) through your sizing. You should get 42,000 normalized tokens and 15 PTUs. If you get anything else, look again at the busiest-minute numbers and the rounding.

learn:stops.a:
**When does PTU sizing stop working?**

**1. Traffic that spikes rarely.** You size from the busiest minute, so a short daily spike means paying for idle capacity all the other hours. Billing can't be paused, so this gets expensive. Stay on pay-per-token, or buy a small PTU base and let spillover send the extra requests to pay-per-token.

**2. A different model or deployment type.** The output weight, the tokens one PTU handles, the minimum and the step size all change. For `gpt-4.1`, "minimum 15, then steps of 5" holds only on Global or Data Zone, while Regional starts at 50 and goes up in steps of 50. Look up the numbers for your exact model and deployment type before you divide and round.

**3. Usage that changes over time.** Agents often add tool calls and longer answers, so output tokens grow and each one counts several times. Last month's busiest minute can quietly become too small. Measure the busiest minute again regularly and resize, and delete deployments you no longer use.

learn:term.a:
**Spillover** is a backup plan for when your reserved capacity is full.

Think of a company car park with spaces kept just for your team. On a normal day, everyone fits. If the car park ever fills up, extra cars go to the public pay-per-hour lot next door. Nobody gets turned away. They just pay as they go for that visit.

In this lesson, the reserved spaces are your **PTU deployment**, the model capacity you pay for every hour. The public lot is a **pay-per-token deployment**, where you pay only for the tokens you use. With spillover turned on, when the PTU deployment is full, extra requests go to the pay-per-token deployment instead of failing.

In the lesson's example, you size from the busiest minute: 42,000 normalized tokens, which rounds up to 15 PTUs. Fifteen PTUs handle 15 × 3,000 = 45,000 a minute. If traffic ever goes past that, spillover sends the extra requests to pay per token. Those extra requests are billed per token on top of the PTU cost.

judge.notes: The car-park analogy calls the overflow lot 'pay-per-hour', but in the lesson hourly billing belongs to the PTU (reserved) side and the overflow is pay per token; the answer also uses 'normalized tokens' without explaining it and includes the arithmetic '15 × 3,000 = 45,000'.

check:0:1.q: Why not “Output tokens cost less than input tokens, per …”?
check:0:1.a:
That option fails in two ways.

First, it is usually not even true. On most price lists, output tokens (the words the model writes) cost *more* per token than input tokens (the words you send in), not less.

Second, even if it were true, it would not explain the mistake. The teammate's error is about *how many* tokens get used, not what each token costs. Pricing per token only matters after you have the right count. And their count is wrong.

Here is why. On step 1 the agent sends the first context. On step 2 it sends that again, plus step 1's answer and tool result. Each later step resends everything before it, so each input is bigger than the last. Six steps cost far more than six copies of the first call. It is like an email thread where every reply quotes everything above it.

"Each step resends everything that earlier steps added" is better because it names the real cause: the input grows every step, so the teammate's count was too low.

judge.notes: The claim that output tokens usually cost more than input tokens is not in the lesson, but it is true in practice and does not contradict the lesson, so I let it pass.

check:0:2.q: Why not “The first call is always the most expensive step”?
check:0:2.a:
That option points the wrong way. The first call is actually the *cheapest* step, not the most expensive.

Here is why. On the first call, the context is only the instructions and the question. The context is everything the agent sends to the model. After that call, the model's answer and any tool result get added to the context. On the next call, the agent sends all of it again, plus the new parts. So each call reads more input tokens than the one before.

In the lesson's example, the calls read 4000, then 5000, then 6000 tokens. The first call is the smallest one.

The option does get one thing right. It notices that the calls don't all cost the same. But it guesses the wrong direction. If the first call really were the biggest, "6 times the first call" would be too high. In fact it is too low, because every later step costs more than the first.

"Each step resends everything that earlier steps added" is better because it names the real mistake: the input keeps growing, so six steps cost more than six first calls.

judge.notes: No significant problems; it is near the length limit, and 'cheapest' refers to input tokens, which matches the lesson's example.

check:1:1.q: Why not “That one call, times the price list”?
check:1:1.a:
That option gets one thing right. The price list really is how you turn tokens into dollars. That part stays.

What it misses is that an agent doesn't make one call per task. It makes many. On every step it resends the whole **context**, meaning the instructions, the question, and every earlier answer and tool result. So each call is bigger than the one before. In the lesson's example, three steps read 4000, then 5000, then 6000 tokens. That adds up to 15000, not 4000.

One test call can't show you that growth. It also can't show spread. Hard tasks take more steps, so some runs cost far more than others. In the research system, a team of agents used about 15 times the tokens of a plain chat. Pricing from one call would miss most of the bill.

The right answer is "Whole runs on real tasks, from traces." A **trace** is the record of each step an agent took, including its token counts. It's better because it measures what a full task actually costs, and it gives you a low, typical and high count to price from.

judge.notes: No real problems; the only loose spots are 'not 4000' (the lesson contrasts 15000 with 12000) and 'miss most of the bill', which stretches the 15x team figure.

check:1:2.q: Why not “A plain chat with the same model”?
check:1:2.a:
A plain chat gets one thing right. It uses the same model, so the price per token is the same. That part of your sum would be correct.

What it misses is how an agent actually works. A plain chat is roughly one question and one answer. An agent loops. On every step it resends the whole **context**: the instructions, the question, every earlier answer and every tool result. So the input gets bigger each step, and a plain chat never shows that growth.

The lesson's numbers show how big the gap is. One agent used about 4 times the tokens of a plain chat. A team of agents used about 15 times. If you priced from a plain chat, your estimate could be several times too low.

A plain chat also gives you only one number. Hard tasks take more steps, so you need a low, typical and high count.

"Whole runs on real tasks, from traces" is better because **traces** (the step-by-step records your POC saves) capture every step's tokens on real work, including the growing context and the spread from easy tasks to hard ones.

check:2:0.q: Why not “Only the easy count, the usual case”?
check:2:0.a:
"Only the easy count" gets one thing right. It uses a real number, measured from real tasks in the POC (your trial build). And if easy tasks really are common, that number does describe many runs.

But it hides the expensive end. Hard tasks took 12 steps, not 3. On every step the agent resends the whole context (everything so far). So each extra step costs more than the one before. A 12-step task costs much more than four times a 3-step task.

If you report only the easy count, your budget looks small and safe. Then the hard tasks arrive and the real bill is far higher. Also, nothing in the question says easy tasks are the usual case. Calling them "usual" is a guess.

Pricing should cover the whole spread of real runs, not the cheapest slice.

"A low, a typical and a high count" is the right answer. It shows the cheap case, the normal case and the worst case, so the price you plan for matches what hard tasks will actually cost.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Only the hardest, to be safe”?
check:2:2.a:
"Only the hardest, to be safe" gets one thing right. Hard tasks really do cost more. A 12-step run resends a much bigger context each step than a 3-step run, so its token count is far higher. Knowing that worst case helps you set a ceiling on spending.

But reporting only that number misleads people. Most of the 20 tasks may have been easy. If you price every task as if it took 12 steps, your estimate could be several times too high. A budget that inflated can make a good project look too expensive to build.

It also hides the spread. The people reading your report can't tell whether hard tasks happen once in a while or all the time. That mix is what decides the real monthly bill.

And "the hardest" is only the hardest of 20. Real users may send something harder still, so this number isn't truly "safe" either.

A low, a typical and a high count is the better answer, because it shows the usual cost and the full range together, so people can plan for the normal case and still prepare for the expensive one.

explain:gotcha.q: Why does “Price the whole run, not one call” matter?
explain:gotcha.a:
When you test an agent, it's tempting to send one request, note its token count, and multiply by the number of tasks you expect. That estimate is always too low.

An agent works in steps. On each step it resends the whole **context**: the instructions, the question, and every earlier answer and tool result. So each step reads more than the one before.

A small example: the first call reads 4,000 tokens. Price from that, and you plan for 4,000 per task. But a three-step run reads 4,000, then 5,000, then 6,000. That's 15,000 tokens, nearly four times your plan. Hard tasks take more steps, so they cost even more.

In real work, the budget runs out early. Someone gets a surprise bill. A product that looked cheap can turn out to lose money on every user.

So price from whole runs. An **MLflow trace** is a step-by-step record of one run, and it adds up the tokens of every call for you. Measure several real tasks, then give a low, typical and high count.

judge.notes: No real problems. The 'always too low' claim is a little strong, and the answer is close to the 200-word limit.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “A running total that grows” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second answer**

*The problem.* An agent doesn't send only the new bit on each step. It resends the whole context: the instructions, the question, every earlier answer and every tool result. So the price of one call badly underestimates the price of a task. (A token is a small chunk of text. Models count and charge by tokens.)

*The idea.* Picture an email thread where every reply quotes everything above it. Each step reads the full thread, then the thread grows. Start at 4,000 tokens and run three steps: the agent reads 4,000, then 5,000, then 6,000. That's 15,000 in, not 12,000.

*The edge case.* Hard tasks take more steps, and each extra step costs more than the last. So I measure whole runs from traces on real tasks and give low, typical and high counts. I also set `recursion_limit` so a stuck agent can't loop up a huge bill.

**Likely follow-up**

"How would you cut that cost?"

Hint: shrink what gets resent. Summarise old tool results, keep only recent messages, and cap the step count. Then name the trade-off: dropping context can make the agent forget something it needs.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- **The bill beats the estimate.** Your budget said one amount. The real invoice is several times higher. That usually means someone priced one call and multiplied by the number of steps.
- **Every step looks the same size.** In your numbers, each step's input is the same. In a real agent, each step's input should be bigger than the last, because it carries everything before it.
- **The estimate is one number.** There is no low, typical and high. Hard tasks take more steps, and each extra step costs more than the one before. So a single number hides the expensive runs.
- **Long runs surprise you.** Some tasks hit the `recursion_limit` (the cap on how many steps a run may take). Those runs cost far more than your "typical" figure.

**The quickest check**

Open one trace (the step-by-step record of a run) from a real task. Look at the input tokens for each step. They should climb, like 4000, then 5000, then 6000. Add them up. If that total is clearly bigger than your estimate for the run, the estimate skipped the growth.

learn:stops.a:
The simple "resend everything" sum is a good starting model. Here are three places where real runs behave differently.

**1. Prompt caching.** Some model providers store the start of a prompt they have already seen. They then charge less for those repeated tokens. Your token count still grows each step, but the dollar cost grows more slowly. Check the price list for a separate "cached input" price, and read cached tokens from your traces.

**2. Long runs hit the context window.** The context window is the most text a model can read at once. Long agent runs often trim old messages or swap them for a short summary. So the context stops growing in a straight line. Measure real traces instead of trusting the simple sum.

**3. Teams of agents.** In a multi-agent system, each helper agent usually starts with its own fresh, smaller context. That means there is not one single growing thread. Add up each agent's whole run separately, then combine them. This is how a team can reach about 15 times the tokens of a plain chat.

judge.notes: Passes. Minor: items 1 and 3 run to four sentences against the two-to-three limit, and the claim that separate agent runs explain the 15x figure is plausible but not stated in the lesson.

learn:term.a:
An **agent** is a program that uses an AI model to finish a task in several steps, not just one reply.

Think of an assistant handling a request. They think, look something up, read what they found, then decide what to do next. They repeat this until the job is done. The twist: the model remembers nothing between calls. So every time the assistant asks it something, they hand over the whole folder so far.

Each round is one **step**. In a step the model writes something, often a request to use a **tool**. A tool is a helper the agent can call, like a search or a database lookup. The tool's reply then gets added to the folder.

In the lesson's example, each pair in `steps` is one agent step:

- `out` is what the model wrote in that step.
- `tool` is what the tool sent back.
- The last step, `[500, 0]`, is the final answer. No tool is used, so its tool result is `0`.

In the LangChain snippet, `graph` is the agent itself. `recursion_limit` caps how many steps it may take.

judge.notes: Minor: the claim that [500, 0] is the final answer with no tool is an inference the lesson never states, but it fits the example.

check:0:0.q: Why not “A model that is half the price per token”?
check:0:0.a:
Halving the price per token sounds like a big cut, and it does save money. A **token** is a small chunk of text, and you pay for every token the model reads and writes. So a cheaper model really does lower the model bill.

The catch is how small that bill is. In the HR assistant, the model costs $900 a month. Half of that is $450 a month. Over 24 months, you save $10,800. That is about 5% of the $214,600 total.

It also carries a risk. A cheaper model may give weaker answers. Then more answers need a person to check or redo them, and that is the costly line.

Checking costs $3,500 a month, or $84,000 over two years. It is the single biggest item, bigger than the whole build team. Cutting it by half saves $42,000, nearly four times what the cheaper model saves.

**Fewer answers that need a person to check them** is better because it shrinks the biggest item, and the biggest item is where a saving matters most.

judge.notes: No significant problems: the figures check out ($450 a month, $10,800 saved, about 5% of $214,600; checking $84,000, half is $42,000, about 3.9 times as much), it is about 175 words, and it gives no solution code.

check:0:2.q: Why not “A cheaper security review before launch”?
check:0:2.a:
A cheaper security review does save money. It is a real line in the build costs. But it is small, and you only pay it once.

In the example, the security review costs $5,000 in total. Even if you cut it in half, you save $2,500. That is barely more than 1% of the $214,600 total.

It also carries a risk. The security review is where someone checks that the assistant won't leak private HR data. Skimping there to save a little money is a poor trade.

Now look at checking. "Checking" means people reading the assistant's answers and fixing the wrong ones. It costs $3,500 every month. Over 24 months, that is $84,000. That one line costs more than the whole build team. If fewer answers need checking, say half as many, you save about $42,000.

This is the lesson's main point. Find the biggest single item first, because that is where a saving matters most.

"Fewer answers that need a person to check them" is better because it shrinks the largest cost, and that saving repeats every month for the system's whole life.

check:1:0.a:
"Tokens for each question" is a real cost, and it belongs on your list. It just isn't paid once.

A **token** is a small piece of text, roughly part of a word. The model provider bills you for every token the model reads and writes. Each time someone asks the assistant something, you pay for the answer's tokens. You also pay for embedding the question. An **embedding** turns text into a list of numbers so the system can search for similar documents.

So this cost comes back every time a question arrives. If 5,000 questions come in this month, you pay for 5,000. Next month you pay again. That makes it a **Run** cost, part of the monthly "LLM calls" line. It grows as more people use the assistant.

The question asks which cost happens only once. Tokens per question repeat for the whole life of the system, so they don't fit.

"Indexing all the documents at first" is better because you prepare and embed the full document set a single time at the start, which makes it a one-off cost.

check:1:2.a:
"Searching the vector index" is an easy one to mix up, because it involves the same index that gets built once.

A **vector index** is where your documents are stored as lists of numbers, so the system can quickly find the chunks that best match a question. Building it and searching it are two different jobs.

Searching happens every time someone asks a question. The assistant turns the question into numbers (an **embedding**), looks up matching chunks, and only then calls the model. More questions mean more searches. On top of that, the search service, such as Azure AI Search or Databricks Vector Search, is billed every month for as long as it runs. So searching is a **run** cost. It keeps coming back.

The option does get one thing right. The index really is part of your costs. It just lands in the monthly group, not the one-off group.

"Indexing all the documents at first" is the better answer because you chunk and embed the whole document collection once at the start. After that, only new documents need embedding.

check:2:0.a:
"Build, paid once" is a fair first guess. The eval set really does start there. The lesson lists "building the eval set" as a build cost. An eval set is your collection of test questions with known good answers, used to check how well the system does. Making it the first time is one-off work, done before launch.

But the question isn't about making the eval set. It's about rerunning it. That happens each time the model or the prompt changes. A model provider might release a new version. You might tweak a prompt to fix a bad answer. Each change means someone runs the evals again to make sure nothing broke.

Those changes keep coming for as long as the system is live. So the cost isn't paid once. It returns again and again, month after month. If you put it under build, your total would leave out that ongoing effort. It would also look smaller than it really is.

"Maintain, keeping it working" is better because rerunning evals is repeated work that keeps the system healthy for its whole life, which is exactly what that group covers.

check:2:1.a:
"Run, paid every month" gets one thing right. Rerunning evals is a cost that keeps coming back, and it does use tokens and compute. (Evals, short for evaluations, are your set of test questions with known good answers. You use them to check the system still behaves.)

What it misses is **why** the cost happens. Run costs come from the system doing its job for users. Each question someone asks burns model tokens, uses hosting, hits the vector search index and may need a person to check the answer. More users means more run cost.

Rerunning evals does not serve any user. It happens because something changed, like a new model version or an edited prompt. Then you need to confirm nothing broke. That work tracks how often you change things, not how busy the system is. It sits beside updating prompts and having someone on call.

Keeping the groups separate helps your total cost of ownership. You can see what grows with traffic and what grows with change.

"Maintain, keeping it working" is better because rerunning evals is upkeep caused by changes to the system, not the cost of answering users.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “One-off plus monthly times months” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**Your 30-second answer**

*The problem.* "People often price an AI system by its token bill. A token is a small chunk of text the model charges for. That bill is often the smallest part. The real cost includes building the system, running it, and keeping it working."

*The idea.* "Total cost of ownership is the one-off build costs, plus every monthly cost times the number of months you plan to run it. For two years, that's 24 months. Then I look at the biggest single item, because that's where a saving matters most."

*A trade-off.* "The biggest item is often people, not the model. In one HR assistant example, staff checking answers cost more over two years than the whole build team. So a pricier model that cuts checking time can still save money."

**A likely follow-up**

"What changes if the system only runs for six months?"

Hint: fewer months means the one-off build costs weigh much more, so a big build may never pay back. Also note that monthly costs can grow over time as more questions and documents arrive.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs that the cost picture was skipped or done wrong**

- **The bill beats the business case.** The estimate only counted model tokens, but the real cloud invoice is several times higher. Hosting, the vector search index (the store that finds matching document chunks) and monitoring were left out.
- **People's time is missing.** Staff spend hours each week checking and redoing answers, but no line in the budget covers it. Often this is the biggest cost of all.
- **Costs creep up every month.** Storage for traces (the saved record of each request) keeps growing, or embeddings for new documents pile up, and nobody planned for it.
- **One-offs and monthlies are mixed up.** The first indexing run gets counted as a monthly cost, or the monthly lines never get multiplied across the full life of the system.
- **Savings land in the wrong place.** The team cuts the token spend but leaves the much bigger costs untouched.

**Quickest check**

Put last month's real invoices and timesheets next to the estimate, one line at a time. Find the biggest real item. Then ask whether the estimate included it at all.

learn:stops.a:
**When the simple "one-off plus monthly times months" rule needs extra care:**

**1. Usage grows over time.** The rule assumes each month costs the same. A popular assistant gets more questions and more documents each month, so tokens, search and checking all rise. Estimate cost per query and per document instead, then multiply by a forecast of volume for each year.

**2. Prices or models change.** Model prices often drop, and you may switch models halfway through. Each switch brings a one-off cost too, like re-running evals and re-embedding all documents. Plan for these as extra one-off items at the point you expect them.

**3. A long life, like five years or more.** A dollar spent in year five is worth less to the business than one spent today. Finance teams handle this with "discounting," which means shrinking future costs by a yearly rate. Ask what rate they use, and treat the plain sum as a rough first number.

Also remember that the biggest item is not always the easiest to cut. Check whether that saving is actually possible.

judge.notes: Passes all checks. Minor: it brings in outside ideas (falling model prices, discounting) and calls eval re-runs one-off, whereas the lesson lists them as monthly maintenance, but none of this contradicts the lesson.

learn:term.a:
**Maintain** means the work of keeping the system working well after it is built. It is not running it. It is looking after it.

Think of a car. Fuel is a running cost, because you pay it just to drive. Servicing is maintenance. You pay a mechanic every so often so the car keeps working as parts wear out or things change.

In this lesson, Maintain is a monthly cost made of three things:

- **Re-running evals.** An eval is a test set of questions with known good answers. When the model or the prompt (the instructions you give the model) changes, you run the tests again to check nothing broke.
- **Updating prompts** when answers drift or needs change.
- **Someone on call**, meaning a person ready to fix problems when they come up.

Now look at the HR assistant example. Its `monthly` lines are `model`, `hosting`, `monitoring` and `checking`. Those are all **Run** costs. Even `checking` is Run, because it is people checking and redoing answers.

So the example has no Maintain lines. In a real business case you would add them as extra monthly lines. That would push the 24-month total higher.

check:0:1.q: Why not “It grows by about 6 percent”?
check:0:1.a:
"It grows by about 6 percent" gets one thing right. The *data* does grow by about 6 percent. Going from 34 GB to 36 GB is 2 GB more, and 2 divided by 34 is roughly 0.06.

What it misses is how the bill is worked out. Search services don't charge per gigabyte. They charge for whole **units**. A unit is a fixed block of capacity that runs every hour, whether you use all of it or not. Here each unit holds 35 GB.

At 34 GB, everything fits in one unit. At 36 GB, one unit is 1 GB short. You can't buy a sliver of a unit, so you need a second whole one. On Azure AI Search S1, that's a jump from about $245 a month to about $490.

So the bill doesn't follow the data smoothly. It stays flat, then jumps a full step when you cross a unit's limit. It's like hotel rooms: one extra guest can mean booking a whole extra room.

"It doubles: you need a second unit" is better because it follows the real billing rule, whole units rounded up, rather than the raw size of the data.

check:0:2.q: Why not “Nothing until you reach 70 GB”?
check:0:2.a:
"Nothing until you reach 70 GB" gets one thing right. Two units hold up to 70 GB. So once you have two units, the bill stays flat all the way from 36 GB to 70 GB.

But it puts the step in the wrong place. The step is not at 70 GB. It is just past 35 GB. A unit is a fixed block of capacity that you pay for every hour it runs. Each unit holds 35 GB. At 34 GB you fit in one unit. At 36 GB you are 1 GB over, and you cannot buy a fraction of a unit. You must add a whole second one, at about $245 a month.

Think of hotel rooms with 2 guests to a room. When the third guest arrives, you book a second room. You don't wait until guest four fills it. Going past 70 GB is like guest five showing up. That is when a third room, or a third unit, is needed.

"It doubles: you need a second unit" is better because the bill jumps from one unit to two the moment your vectors outgrow the first 35 GB.

check:1:1.a:
"It stays the same" gets two things right. You still have the same 5 million chunks. And each number in a vector still takes 4 bytes.

What it misses is the middle part of the formula. Space is chunks times dimensions times 4 bytes. "Dimensions" just means how many numbers are in each vector. Going from 1,536 to 3,072 means every vector now holds twice as many numbers. Each chunk is the same text, but its vector is twice as long.

Here is the sum both ways:

- 5,000,000 × 1,536 × 4 = 30,720,000,000 bytes, about 30.7 GB
- 5,000,000 × 3,072 × 4 = 61,440,000,000 bytes, about 61.4 GB

That change matters for the bill too. 30.7 GB fits in one 35 GB S1 partition. 61.4 GB needs two, so you pay for a whole extra unit.

"It doubles" is better because dimensions is one of the multipliers, so doubling it doubles the total space.

check:1:2.a:
"It halves" gets one thing right. The size does change by a factor of two. But it gets the direction backwards.

A "dimension" is just one number in a vector. Going from 1,536 to 3,072 dimensions means every vector now holds twice as many numbers. Each number still takes 4 bytes. So each vector takes twice the bytes, not half.

The number of chunks stays the same at 5 million. Only the numbers per vector changed. Here is the lesson's formula for both cases:

- 5,000,000 × 1,536 × 4 = 30,720,000,000 bytes, about 30.7 GB
- 5,000,000 × 3,072 × 4 = 61,440,000,000 bytes, about 61.4 GB

The space goes up. It does not go down.

A mix-up may come from thinking a bigger model packs data more tightly. It doesn't. More dimensions just means a longer list of numbers to store.

"It doubles" is better because the space equals chunks times dimensions times 4 bytes, so doubling the dimensions with the same chunks doubles the space.

check:2:1.a:
"Nothing, because nobody searched" sounds fair. Some cloud services do charge per use, such as paying for each API call. So linking cost to activity is a reasonable instinct.

A search endpoint doesn't work that way. An endpoint is a server set up to answer searches. To answer fast, it keeps your vectors loaded and ready all the time. Keeping that server running costs money whether anyone asks a question or not.

That's why the lesson says you pay for capacity, not use. Capacity means how much the service is set up to hold and handle. On Databricks AI Search Standard, one unit costs $0.28 an hour. Over a month that's about $204, even with zero searches.

So a forgotten test endpoint is a quiet, steady cost. If you're not using one, delete it.

"It still bills every hour it exists" is the better answer because it matches how these services actually charge: for the hours the endpoint is kept running, not for the searches it answers.

check:2:2.q: Why not “Only the space the vectors take”?
check:2:2.a:
"Only the space the vectors take" sounds sensible. Many cloud services do charge like that: you pay a little for each gigabyte you store. So it gets one thing right. The size of your vectors does matter, because it decides how many units you need.

But that's not how search services bill. You don't pay per gigabyte. You pay for **units**, which are blocks of capacity the service keeps switched on for you. Each unit has a price per hour. It is charged whether you use it or not.

For Databricks AI Search on Standard, one unit costs $0.28 an hour. That's about $204 a month. The endpoint is the running service that answers your searches. If nobody searches it for a whole month, it still runs, so you still pay about $204 for each unit. A small set of vectors doesn't make that cheaper. You still pay for at least one whole unit.

"It still bills every hour it exists" is the better answer because the cost comes from keeping the endpoint running, not from how much it stores or how often anyone searches it.

judge.notes: No major problems. The closing line says cost is 'not from how much it stores', which sits slightly awkwardly beside the earlier point that vector size decides the number of units, but it does not contradict the lesson.

explain:interview.q: How do I explain “Work out the size, then round up to whole units” in an interview?
explain:interview.a:
**A 30-second spoken answer**

*The problem:* "Vector search services don't bill by the gigabyte. They bill whole units of capacity. Each unit runs every hour, even if nobody searches."

*The idea:* "So I work out the size first: number of vectors, times dimensions, times 4 bytes. Dimensions just means how many numbers are in each vector. Six million vectors of 3,072 numbers is about 73.7 GB. Then I divide by what one unit holds and round up. With 35 GB units, 73.7 divided by 35 is 2.1, so that's 3 units, not 2.1."

*The edge case:* "The bill moves in steps. Growing from 34 GB to 36 GB doesn't add a small cost. It adds a whole unit."

**A likely follow-up**

"How would you bring that bill down?"

*Hint at a strong answer:* Shrink the vectors. OpenAI's newer models let you ask for fewer numbers per vector, such as 256 instead of 3,072. That can drop you a whole unit or more. Then name the trade-off: quality may dip a little. So you'd test on your eval set first. An eval set is a fixed list of test questions with known good answers. You could also add that idle endpoints should be shut down, since they bill every hour.

judge.notes: No real problems: the figures (73.7 GB, 2.1, 3 units, 34→36 GB step) match the lesson, and the whole answer is only about 200 words, with a shorter spoken part.

learn:spot.q: How would I spot it going wrong?
learn:spot.a:
**Warning signs**

- The bill is a whole unit higher than you planned. Someone likely counted units as fractions, like 2.1. Services only sell whole units.
- The bill jumps after a small data load. A few extra chunks pushed you just past one unit's limit.
- You switched from `text-embedding-3-small` to `text-embedding-3-large`, and storage doubled without anyone planning for it.
- An old endpoint still shows charges every month. An endpoint is the running search service. It bills every hour it exists, even if nobody searches it.
- You shrank vectors to save space, and then answers got worse in real use. That means nobody tested quality on your eval set first. An eval set is your fixed list of test questions with known good answers.

**Quickest check**

Open the search service's usage or billing page. Compare two things with your plan: the storage it reports and the number of units it bills.

If the storage is far off, check two inputs first. Check the dimension count, which is how many numbers each vector holds. Then check how many bytes each number takes. Those are the most common slips.

judge.notes: It overclaims: 'That means nobody tested quality' doesn't follow, since the lesson says quality may drop a little even after shrinking, and 'the most common slips' is not in the lesson.

learn:stops.a:
The simple rule works well for rough planning. Here are three places where it needs extra care.

**The index stores more than the raw vectors.** Services keep extra data so search is fast: a lookup structure linking similar vectors, plus the chunk text and metadata (extra labels like source or date). Real usage can be well above vectors times dimensions times 4 bytes. Check the service's reported index size, and leave spare room.

**The vectors are compressed.** Some services can store each number in 1 byte, or even 1 bit, instead of 4. This is called quantization. If it is on, the 4-byte rule overstates the space. Use the byte size the service actually stores.

**The data keeps changing.** If you switch to a new embedding model, you usually keep the old and new indexes running side by side for a while. That can double your units during the move. Steady growth also pushes you over a step sooner than you expect. Plan for next year's size, not today's.

learn:term.a:
Without this idea, cloud bills surprise you. Here is a realistic case.

A team stores 30 GB of vectors on Azure AI Search. One S1 unit holds 35 GB, so they pay about $245 a month. They plan a budget by gigabytes: "we're at 30 GB, so a bit more data costs a bit more money."

Then they switch from `text-embedding-3-small` to `text-embedding-3-large` for better answers. Each vector now has twice as many numbers, so the data jumps to about 60 GB. That no longer fits in one unit. They need two, and the bill doubles to about $490 a month. The search results got a little better, but the cost doubled overnight.

A "unit" is a fixed block of capacity you rent by the hour, whether anyone uses it or not. You can't rent half of one.

If they had first multiplied vectors by numbers per vector by 4 bytes, then rounded up to whole units, they'd have seen the jump coming. They could also have tried shorter vectors and checked quality on their eval set, which is their own set of test questions with known good answers.

judge.notes: The numbers match the lesson (30 GB fits one 35 GB S1 unit at $245; large vectors double the size to 60 GB, which needs 2 units at about $490). It is plain, about 200 words, and gives no solution code.
